# Dot actions and Hessenberg spaces for dihedral groups

**Authors:** Jonathan Boretsky Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, McGill University, Montreal, QC Email address: jonathan.boretsky@mcgill.ca , Reuven Hodges Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045 Email address: rmhodges@ku.edu , Nathan Lesnevich Address: Department of Mathematics, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK 74078 Email address: nlesnev@okstate.edu , Tyrrell McAllister Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, 82071 Email address: tmcallis@uwyo.edu and Joseph Pappe Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA 22904 Email address: yyz8xu@virginia.edu

## Abstract

Splines on Weyl groups model the equivariant cohomology of regular semisimple Hessenberg varieties, and the natural group action on them encodes the monodromy action. The resulting representations are of great interest in algebraic combinatorics for their connections to Hecke algebra characters, LLT polynomials, and chromatic symmetric functions. We study the analogous construction for dihedral groups, which in general have no underlying geometry. Using purely algebraic methods, we show that these spline modules are free, construct explicit bases, and compute their Hilbert series, recovering the familiar properties of the geometric setting. We also determine the associated dihedral group representations completely. Unlike what is conjectured for the symmetric group case, these need not be permutation representations.

## 1. Introduction

Let $I_{2}(n)$ , with $n\geq 3$ , be the dihedral group of order $2n$ , with root system $\Phi$ embedded in $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ . A Hessenberg space $H$ is a lower order ideal in the poset of positive roots $\Phi^{+}$ . We insist that $H$ contain the simple roots. Each root $\gamma\in\Phi$ is naturally associated to both a linear form $t_{\gamma}$ in the polynomials $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ and a reflection $s_{\gamma}$ in $I_{2}(n)$ . As such, the module of splines given by $H$ is defined to be the set

$$ \mathcal{M}_{H}=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}(\mathcal{M}_{H})_{i}\coloneqq\left\{\left.\overline{\rho}\in\!\!\!\prod_{w\in I_{2}(n)}\!\!\mathbb{C}[x,y]\;\right|\;\overline{\rho}(w)-\overline{\rho}(ws_{\gamma})\in\left\langle t_{w(\gamma)}\right\rangle\text{ for all }w\in I_{2}(n),\,\gamma\in H\right\} $$

with (graded) $I_{2}(n)$ -module structure $(w\cdot\overline{\rho})(v)=w(\overline{\rho}(w^{-1}v))$ and (graded) $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module structure given by multiplication.

The module of splines is of particular interest in geometric combinatorics for its connections to chromatic symmetric functions and certain subvarieties of the flag variety. Indeed, if $W$ is a Weyl group and $H$ a Hessenberg space, then the corresponding module of splines is isomorphic to the $T$ -equivariant cohomology of the associated regular semisimple Hessenberg variety. The connection between this combinatorial module and this geometric object is called GKM theory [17]. In this Weyl group case, the ring structure is the cohomology ring structure, the module structure is over the equivariant cohomology of a point, and the $W$ -module structure is equivalent to the monodromy action [4, 9].

Now the dihedral group $I_{2}(n)$ is not crystallographic in general, and thus does not have an associated flag variety, let alone Hessenberg varieties. As such, our methods are entirely algebraic. In spite of this, the module $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ displays remarkable similarities to its geometric counterpart. We prove for example that $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is a free module over the polynomial ring whose Hilbert series is given by an inversion-type statistic on $I_{2}(n)$ , precisely as it is in the geometric case.

#### Theorem 1.

The module $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is a free module over $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . The rank generating function for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is palindromic and given by

$$ P_{H}(q)=\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell_{H}(w)}, $$

where $\ell_{H}(w)$ is the number of roots in $H$ sent to $\Phi^{-}$ by $w$ . Furthermore, the Hilbert series of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is

$$ \Hilb(\mathcal{M}_{H};q)=\frac{P_{H}(q)}{(1-q)^{2}}. $$

Theorem 1 is Corollary 4.7 below.

The freeness of this module in the case that $W$ is a Weyl group is intrinsic to the geometry, and the Hilbert series are given by a Betti number computation. Moreover, this Betti number calculation is given by an affine paving of the associated Hessenberg variety [30, 36]. The associated GKM classes to these pavings are largely unknown. It is an open question in all Weyl types to give explicit cohomology classes that correspond to this paving. While these classes can be described geometrically [6, 7, 13], explicit formulas for their localizations, i.e. for the corresponding splines, are known only in special cases [12, 26]. We give an explicit homogeneous module basis for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ that satisfies precisely the properties that would follow from a paving.

#### Theorem 2.

There exists a homogeneous basis $\{\overline{\rho}_{w}\mid w\in I_{2}(n)\}$ of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ , with $\deg\overline{\rho}_{w}=\ell_{H}(w)$ , such that each $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is either a Schubert spline or has the form

$$ \overline{\rho}_{w}(v)=\begin{cases}c^{w}(v)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in H,\\
vs_{\alpha}\notin G_{w}\end{subarray}}t_{v(\alpha)},&if $v\in G_{w}$,\\[6.0pt]
0,&if $v\notin G_{w}$,\end{cases} $$

where $G_{w}$ contains $w$ and is contained in its Bruhat upper ideal, and $c^{w}(v)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ for every $v\in G_{w}$ .

Theorem 4.5 constructs this basis recursively, Proposition 5.3 describes its supports, and Corollary 5.2 gives the displayed localization formula. The Schubert splines satisfy an analogous product formula in the full reflection graph, given in Theorem 3.4.

Finally, we completely determine the $I_{2}(n)$ -module structure of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . Specifically, we compute the (graded) left and right dot action representations

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\,(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{i}\qquad\qquad\mathrm{R}_{H}=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\,(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{i}, $$

each derived from an equivariant quotient of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . Determining this structure for Weyl groups is a subject of significant research. For the symmetric group, the left and right quotients correspond to passing from equivariant to ordinary cohomology of the regular semisimple Hessenberg variety and its twin, respectively. There, the left representation is, under the Frobenius characteristic map and up to the standard involution $\omega$ on symmetric functions, a chromatic quasisymmetric function [9, 19, 32], and the right representation is similarly a unicellular LLT polynomial [2, 3, 19]. For $W=S_{n}$ , the decomposition of $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ into irreducibles is known [32]. It is a major open problem to determine whether these graded representations are permutation representations of a particular form, i.e. to prove or disprove the graded Stanley–Stembridge Conjecture [9, 19, 32, 34], whose ungraded statement was proven by Hikita [21] and later reproven by Griffin, et al. [18]. A proof of the graded statement has recently been claimed by OpenAI [28].

In other Weyl types, in particular the classical types B/C/D, the $W$ -module structure has received recent attention for its deep connections to Hecke algebras and other geometric and representation-theoretic objects [1, 4, 29, 33]. In these cases, there are no combinatorial formulae that compute the left or right representations in full, and it is an active area of research to find ones [4, 26, 29]. It is also unknown whether these left representations are permutation representations of a particular type [26]. We settle each of these questions in their entirety for $I_{2}(n)$ .

#### Theorem 3.

Let $H\subsetneq\Phi^{+}$ be a Hessenberg space containing the simple roots $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ and let $h=\lfloor\left\lvert H\right\rvert/2\rfloor$ . If $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ is odd, let $\alpha$ be the $H$ -dominant simple root. Then, as an element of the graded representation ring of $I_{2}(n)$ ,

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}\cong\begin{cases}(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{2h-1})\mathbbold{1}\oplus q^{h}\left(C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1}\right)&if $\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h$,\\[10.0pt]
(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{2h})\mathbbold{1}\oplus(q^{h}+q^{h+1})\left(C_{\alpha}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right)&if $\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h+1$\end{cases} $$

and

$$ \mathrm{R}_{H}\cong\begin{cases}\displaystyle\mathsf{Co}_{H}\oplus q^{h}\left(C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1}\right)&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h,\\[10.0pt]
\displaystyle\mathsf{Co}_{H}\oplus q^{h}\left(C_{\alpha}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right)\oplus q^{h+1}\left(C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right)&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h+1.\end{cases} $$

The definition of an $H$ -dominant simple root is Definition 6.2. The irreducible representations $\mathbbold{1}$ and $V_{i}$ as well as the permutation representations $C_{\gamma}$ are defined in Subsection 2.3, whereas $\mathsf{P}_{h}$ is defined in Section 6 and $\mathsf{Co}_{H}$ is defined in Lemma 7.2. Theorem 3 is Theorems 6.4 and 7.3 below. We note that the left representation is not necessarily a permutation representation in Corollary 6.11.

This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides the necessary background. Section 3 treats the case where $H$ is the set of positive roots. This is the Schubert case, corresponding to the Schubert calculus of flag varieties. Much of the content of this section is known in greater generality [5, 24, 25], but our treatment is entirely algebraic and from first principles. Section 4 gives an iterative construction for the bases from Theorem 2. Section 5 computes the properties of this basis, both completing the description of Theorem 2 and setting up the necessary calculations for the following sections. Finally, Section 6 computes the left dot action representation and Section 7 computes the right dot action representation, which together give Theorem 3.

## 2. Background

### 2.1. Vector Algebra

Fix a complex vector space $V\cong\mathbb{C}^{n}$ with symmetric bilinear form $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ given by the bilinear extension of the standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . If $\alpha\in V$ satisfies $\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle\neq 0$ , then the reflection $s_{\alpha}$ across its orthogonal hyperplane is given by

$$ s_{\alpha}(v)=v-\frac{2\left\langle v,\alpha\right\rangle}{\left\langle\alpha,\alpha\right\rangle}\alpha. $$

Let $e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}$ be the standard basis for $V$ . There is a natural map from $V$ to the linear polynomials in $\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$ defined as the linear extension of $e_{i}\mapsto t_{i}$ . For a particular vector $\alpha=\sum c_{i}e_{i}\in V$ , we denote by $t_{\alpha}=\sum c_{i}t_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$ the linear form associated to it by this map. Via this identification, any linear map $X$ on $V$ may be extended to the polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$ by acting on each variable individually: $X$ maps the monomial $\prod_{i}t_{i}^{m_{i}}$ to $\prod_{i}X(t_{i})^{m_{i}}$ , and extends linearly.

#### Example 2.1.

If $V=\mathbb{C}^{2}$ and $\displaystyle X=\begin{bmatrix}[r]-1&1\\ 0&2\end{bmatrix}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle X(t_{1}) \displaystyle=-t_{1} \displaystyle\text{since }X(e_{1})=-e_{1}, \displaystyle X(t_{2}) \displaystyle=t_{1}+2t_{2} \displaystyle\text{since }X(e_{2})=e_{1}+2e_{2}. $$

This action extends multiplicatively to higher degree monomials; for example $X(t_{1}t_{2}^{2})=X(t_{1})X(t_{2})^{2}=(-t_{1})(t_{1}+2t_{2})^{2}$ . It also extends linearly to polynomials; for example, $X(t_{1}+t_{2})=X(t_{1})+X(t_{2})=2t_{2}$ .

#### Lemma 2.2.

Let $s_{\alpha}$ be a reflection on $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ . If $f$ is any polynomial in $\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$ , then $f-s_{\alpha}(f)$ is divisible by $t_{\alpha}$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the action of an arbitrary $X=[c_{ij}]\in\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C})$ on $\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$ . This action interacts with evaluation on $v\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ via:

$$ Xf(v)=f(X^{T}v). $$

It suffices to verify this identity on the generators $t_{j}$ , and certainly

$$ Xt_{j}(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{ij}t_{i}(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{ij}v_{i}=t_{j}(X^{T}v). $$

Since reflections $s_{\alpha}$ are symmetric linear operators, the vanishing set of $f-s_{\alpha}(f)$ contains any point on the reflecting hyperplane $H_{\alpha}=\mathcal{V}(t_{\alpha})$ . Formally, if $v\in H_{\alpha}$ then

$$ s_{\alpha}(f)(v)=f(s_{\alpha}^{T}v)=f(s_{\alpha}v)=f(v). $$

Since $t_{\alpha}$ is irreducible (it is linear), by nullstellensatz $f-s_{\alpha}(f)$ is a multiple of $t_{\alpha}$ . ∎

The remainder of this work considers the dihedral group $I_{2}(n)$ , as naturally extended from its typical $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ embeddings to $V=\mathbb{C}^{2}$ , so the polynomial ring is $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . We continue to use $t_{\alpha}$ to denote the linear polynomial corresponding to the vector $\alpha$ .

### 2.2. The Dihedral Group and Root Systems

The dihedral group

$$ I_{2}(n)\coloneq\left\langle s_{1},s_{2}\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\middle|\allowbreak\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\mathopen{}s_{1}^{2}=s_{2}^{2}=(s_{1}s_{2})^{n}=e\right\rangle $$

is the group of symmetries of a regular $n$ -gon. We employ here the definition that gives $I_{2}(n)$ as the finite rank-two Coxeter group of order $2n$ .

The reflections $s_{1}\coloneqq s_{\alpha_{1}}$ and $s_{2}\coloneqq s_{\alpha_{2}}$ form a minimal generating set. For each $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , there is a corresponding set of reduced words, that is, minimal ways of expressing $w$ as a product of $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ . The length of an element $w$ , denoted $\ell(w)$ , is the length of any reduced word for $w$ . Note that reduced words are alternating sequences of $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ since $s_{1}^{2}=s_{2}^{2}=e$ . Every element of the dihedral group has only one reduced word except for the longest element $w_{0}$ , which is of length $n$ and can start with either $s_{1}$ or $s_{2}$ and alternate between them $n$ times, since $(s_{1}s_{2})^{n}=e$ . The Bruhat order $\leq$ on $I_{2}(n)$ is defined letting $w\leq v$ when $w$ appears as a subword of a reduced word for $v$ .

The dihedral group is also an example of a real reflection group. Such groups are generated by reflections $s_{i}=s_{\alpha_{i}}$ across particular hyperplanes defined by normal vectors $\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , called roots. We take all roots to be unit length. A real reflection group corresponds to a real root system $\Phi$ , which is a finite set of real-valued vectors which satisfies the following:

- • if $\alpha\in\Phi$ then $-\alpha\in\Phi$ ,

- • if $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ and $\alpha=c\beta$ then $c=\pm 1$ , and

- • if $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ then $s_{\alpha}(\beta)\in\Phi$ .

The correspondence between real reflection groups and real root systems is that the set of reflections $\{s_{\alpha}\mid\alpha\in\Phi\}$ generates a group, which is a real reflection group. A generic hyperplane will partition $\Phi$ into “positive” roots $\Phi^{+}$ and “negative” roots $\Phi^{-}$ , so that there is a one-to-one correspondence between $\Phi^{+}$ and the reflections. Moreover, the simple roots are the unique pair of positive roots closest to the generic hyperplane, and are always the positive roots that correspond to the generators $s_{1},s_{2}$ . We write $\Delta$ for the set of simple roots.

We index the positive roots of $I_{2}(n)$ so that $s_{1}=s_{\alpha_{1}}$ , $s_{2}=s_{\alpha_{2}}$ , and more generally

$$ (s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}=s_{\alpha_{2k+1}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(s_{2}s_{1})^{k}s_{2}=s_{\alpha_{2k+2}} $$

for $2k+1\leq n$ and $2k+2\leq n$ , respectively. Our proofs will not rely on a particular embedding, but in examples we will often place $\alpha_{2k+1}$ at angle $k\pi/n$ and $\alpha_{2k+2}$ at angle $(n-1-k)\pi/n$ .

#### Example 2.3.

Below, the red lines show reflection symmetries and the arrows show a choice of positive roots for $I_{2}(3)$ , $I_{2}(4)$ , and $I_{2}(5)$ .

For $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , let

$$ N_{L}(w)\coloneq\left\{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\middle|\allowbreak\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\mathopen{}\ell(s_{\alpha}w)<\ell(w)\right\} $$

be the left inversion set of $w$ . Similarly, let

$$ N_{R}(w)\coloneq\left\{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\middle|\allowbreak\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\mathopen{}\ell(ws_{\alpha})<\ell(w)\right\} $$

be the right inversion set of $w$ .

#### Lemma 2.4.

The following hold for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ .

- (1) If $w\notin\{e,w_{0}\}$ , then $w$ has a unique simple left descent and a unique simple left ascent. That is, exactly one of $s_{\alpha_{1}}w,s_{\alpha_{2}}w$ has length $\ell(w)-1$ , and exactly one has length $\ell(w)+1$ .

- (2) If $0<\ell(u)<n$ , then $u\leq v$ if and only if either $v=u$ or $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$ .

- (3) For every $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , one has $\left\lvert N_{L}(w)\right\rvert=\ell(w)$ . If $\alpha\in\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}$ and $\ell(s_{\alpha}w)=\ell(w)+1$ , then $\displaystyle N_{L}(s_{\alpha}w)$ $\displaystyle=\{\alpha\}\sqcup s_{\alpha}N_{L}(w),$ $\displaystyle N_{R}(s_{\alpha}w)$ $\displaystyle=\{w^{-1}(\alpha)\}\sqcup N_{R}(w).$

#### Proof.

Every reduced word in $I_{2}(n)$ is alternating, and for each $1\leq k<n$ the two alternating words of length $k$ represent distinct elements. The two alternating words of length $n$ represent the longest element $w_{0}$ . Hence every element other than $e$ and $w_{0}$ has a unique nonempty reduced word.

Now let $0<\ell(w)<n$ , and write the unique reduced word for $w$ as $w=s_{\alpha_{i}}s_{\alpha_{j}}\cdots$ . Left multiplication by $s_{\alpha_{i}}$ cancels the first letter and lowers length by one. Left multiplication by the other simple reflection gives an alternating word of length $\ell(w)+1\leq n$ , so it raises length by one. This proves (1).

For (2), use the subword criterion for Bruhat order. If $u\leq v$ , then $\ell(u)\leq\ell(v)$ , and equality forces $u=v$ . Thus, if $u\leq v$ , then either $v=u$ or $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$ . Conversely, suppose $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$ . Every alternating reduced word of length $\ell(v)$ contains both alternating words of length $\ell(u)$ as subwords. Thus a reduced word for $u$ occurs as a subword of a reduced word for $v$ , so $u\leq v$ .

For (3), use the usual rank-two inversion criterion: $\ell(s_{\beta}w)<\ell(w)$ if and only if $w^{-1}(\beta)\in\Phi^{-}$ . Thus $N_{L}(w)$ is the set of positive roots sent negative by $w^{-1}$ . A minimal gallery from the fundamental chamber $C$ to the chamber $wC$ crosses exactly $\ell(w)$ reflecting hyperplanes, so $\left\lvert N_{L}(w)\right\rvert=\ell(w)$ . Finally, if $\ell(s_{\alpha}w)=\ell(w)+1$ , then $w^{-1}(\alpha)\in\Phi^{+}$ . Since a simple reflection sends only its own simple root from $\Phi^{+}$ to $\Phi^{-}$ , the positive roots sent negative by $(s_{\alpha}w)^{-1}=w^{-1}s_{\alpha}$ are precisely $\alpha$ , together with the roots $s_{\alpha}\beta$ for $\beta\in N_{L}(w)$ . This is the first line of (3). The same logic applies for $N_{R}(w)$ . ∎

### 2.3. Representations

The representation theory of the dihedral group is very well understood. We record several standard facts here. These can be found, for example, in [Serre, Chapter 5, §5.3], or follow from direct computation.

All irreducible representations of $I_{2}(n)$ are either one- or two-dimensional. If $n$ is odd, then $I_{2}(n)$ has $2$ one-dimensional irreducible representations and $(n-1)/2$ two-dimensional irreducible representations. If $n$ is even, then $I_{2}(n)$ has $4$ one-dimensional irreducible representations and $(n-2)/2$ two-dimensional irreducible representations.

The trivial representation is $\mathbbold{1}(w)\coloneqq(1)$ and the sign representation is $\sgn(w)\coloneqq(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ .

Let $r=s_{1}s_{2}$ . When $n$ is even, let $\eta_{0}$ and $\eta_{1}$ denote the one-dimensional representations determined by

$$ \eta_{0}(r)=-1,\qquad\eta_{0}(s_{1})=1,\qquad\eta_{1}(r)=-1,\qquad\eta_{1}(s_{1})=-1. $$

For each integer $j$ with $1\leq j<n/2$ , let $V_{j}$ denote the two-dimensional irreducible representation of $I_{2}(n)$ whose character is given by

$$ \chi_{V_{j}}(r^{a})=2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi ja}{n}\right),\qquad\chi_{V_{j}}(r^{a}s_{1})=0 $$

for $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ . In particular, $V_{1}$ is the defining representation, which sends $w$ to the element of $\GL_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ that defines it as a symmetry of the $n$ -gon. These, together with the two one-dimensional representations for $n$ odd or the four one-dimensional representations for $n$ even, constitute all of the irreducible representations of $I_{2}(n)$ .

There is one more family of representations, indexed by positive roots, that will be critical for our results. For $\gamma\in\Phi^{+}$ , when $n$ is even let $\eta_{\gamma}$ be the unique representation in $\{\eta_{0},\eta_{1}\}$ satisfying $\eta_{\gamma}(s_{\gamma})=1$ . Let

$$ C_{\gamma}\coloneq\operatorname{Ind}_{\left\langle s_{\gamma}\right\rangle}^{I_{2}(n)}\mathbbold{1} $$

be the permutation representation on the cosets of $\left\langle s_{\gamma}\right\rangle$ . Its irreducible decomposition is

$$ C_{\gamma}\cong\begin{cases}\displaystyle\mathbbold{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{(n-1)/2}V_{j},&n\text{ is odd},\\[12.0pt]
\displaystyle\mathbbold{1}\oplus\eta_{\gamma}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n/2-1}V_{j},&n\text{ is even}.\end{cases} $$

#### Example 2.5.

Consider $I_{2}(4)$ , generated by $s_{1}\coloneqq s_{\alpha_{1}}$ and $s_{2}\coloneqq s_{\alpha_{2}}$ . The longest element is $s_{1}s_{2}s_{1}s_{2}=s_{2}s_{1}s_{2}s_{1}$ . The trivial representation always evaluates to $1$ , so $\mathbbold{1}(s_{1})=\mathbbold{1}(s_{2})=1$ . The sign representation measures the parity of the lengths of words as expressions in $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ , so $\sgn(s_{1})=\sgn(s_{2})=-1$ . Also, $\sgn(s_{\alpha_{3}})=-1$ since $s_{\alpha_{3}}=s_{1}s_{2}s_{1}$ .

Finally, $V_{1}(s_{1})=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$ , since the reflection associated to $\alpha_{1}$ is the reflection across the $y$ -axis, and $V_{1}(s_{2})=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ , since the reflection associated to $\alpha_{2}$ is the reflection across $y=x$ , which swaps $x$ and $y$ .

### 2.4. The Root Poset

For each choice of simple roots in the root system for $I_{2}(n)$ , the positive roots $\Phi^{+}$ have a natural partial order.

#### Definition 2.6.

Let $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ be simple roots. The root poset of $I_{2}(n)$ is the partial order on $\Phi^{+}$ given by $\alpha\leq\beta$ whenever $\beta-\alpha\in\mathrm{Cone}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\coloneqq\{c_{1}\alpha_{1}+c_{2}\alpha_{2}\mid c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\}$ [11].

#### Remark 2.7.

One notable (and standard) property of these root posets is that $\alpha_{i}<\alpha_{j}$ in the root poset if and only if the corresponding reflections satisfy $\ell(s_{\alpha_{i}})<\ell(s_{\alpha_{j}})$ , which is equivalent to $s_{\alpha_{i}}<s_{\alpha_{j}}$ in the strong Bruhat order on $I_{2}(n)$ .

We consider $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ where $H$ is a lower order ideal in the root poset. We always insist that $H$ contain the simple roots $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ . We call such $H$ a Hessenberg space. As such the possible $H$ are:

$$ \begin{matrix}\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{j-1},\alpha_{j}\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\ldots,\alpha_{2k-2},\alpha_{2k}\}\end{matrix} $$

for $j\in\{2,\ldots,n\}$ and $k\in\{2,\ldots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\}$ .

#### Remark 2.8.

Our characterization covers more subsets of roots than it may seem. In particular, any convex subset of positive roots can be written as a Hessenberg space up to a different choice of simple roots. For example in $I_{2}(6)$ , up to sign, the convex subset $\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{3},\alpha_{5}\}$ of positive roots can be made into a Hessenberg space by declaring $\alpha_{3}$ and $-\alpha_{5}$ to be the simple roots. #### Remark 2.9.

Since $I_{2}(n)$ is not crystallographic in general, there are several reasonable ways to define a root poset that do not necessarily coincide. This root poset does not precisely align with the special cases $G_{2}\cong I_{2}(6)$ , $A_{2}\cong I_{2}(3)$ and $B_{2},C_{2}\cong I_{2}(4)$ . For $A_{2}$ the root poset is identical. The root posets $B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ are different, but every lower order ideal for $I_{2}(4)$ is a lower order ideal for the $B_{2}$ or $C_{2}$ root system, and so for our purposes are the same. The root poset for $G_{2}$ is entirely different, as neither family of ideals contains the other, but we do not explore this exceptional group here.

#### Definition 2.10.

Given $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ , the $H$ -inversion set of $w\in I_{2}(n)$ is

$$ \mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)\coloneqq\{\alpha\in H\mid\ell(ws_{\alpha})<\ell(w)\}=H\cap N_{R}(w). $$

The map $\alpha\mapsto-w(\alpha)$ identifies $\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)$ with $w(-H)\cap\Phi^{+}$ . The $H$ -length is

$$ \ell_{H}(w)=\left\lvert\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)\right\rvert. $$

Given $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ , the associated Cayley graph is the graph with $I_{2}(n)$ as its vertices and $\{(w,ws_{\alpha})\mid\alpha\in H\}$ as its edges. We impose two additional structures: first and foremost the labeled Cayley graph $\mathcal{G}_{H}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}_{H},\mathcal{L})$ has vertices $\mathcal{V}=I_{2}(n)$ , edges $\mathcal{E}_{H}=\{(w,ws_{\alpha})\mid w\in I_{2}(n),\;\alpha\in H\}$ and edge labeling $\mathcal{L}\colon\mathcal{E}_{H}\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ given by $\mathcal{L}(w,ws_{\alpha})\coloneqq t_{w(\alpha)}$ (up to multiplication by a unit).

On the left, we have $\mathrm{inv}_{H}(s_{2}s_{1})=\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{3}\}$ .

Second, the Cayley graph has a natural acyclic orientation by insisting that edges are directed from elements of lesser length to elements of greater length. In this case $\ell_{H}(w)$ is the in-degree of $w$ in this directed graph.

As such, there is a natural partial order $\prec_{H}$ given by the transitive closure of $w\prec_{H}ws_{\alpha}$ for all $\alpha\in H$ where $\ell(w)<\ell(ws_{\alpha})$ .

When $H=\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}$ , this is the right weak Bruhat order on $I_{2}(n)$ . When $H=\Phi^{+}$ , this is the strong Bruhat order on $I_{2}(n)$ .

### 2.5. Splines and their Algebraic Properties

Given a subset $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ of roots whose associated reflections generate $I_{2}(n)$ , the set of splines is:

$$ \mathcal{M}_{H}\coloneqq\left\{\overline{\rho}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]\mid\overline{\rho}(w)-\overline{\rho}(ws_{\alpha})\in\left\langle t_{w(\alpha)}\right\rangle,\text{ for all }w\in I_{2}(n),\;\;\alpha\in H\right\}. $$

We will always insist that $H$ is a Hessenberg space. This construction is more easily seen as a generalized spline on the labeled Cayley graph $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ . An element of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is an assignment of polynomials to vertices of $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ such that the difference of two polynomials along an edge is divisible by the label on that edge. The following are some splines on $I_{2}(3)$ with $H=\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}\}$ . The labels are given by the positive root $\alpha$ instead of the polynomials $t_{\alpha}$ for readability.

The following are some splines on $I_{2}(4)$ with $H=\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}$ .

Note that $\mathcal{L}(w,ws_{\alpha})=t_{\beta}$ precisely when $s_{\beta}w=ws_{\alpha}$ .

#### Lemma 2.14.

The set of splines is a ring with pointwise multiplication and addition.

#### Proof.

We may simply check this for two $\overline{\rho},\overline{\sigma}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ at an arbitrary pair $(w,ws_{\alpha})$ . For $\overline{\rho}+\overline{\sigma}$ , this is straightforward. As for the product $\overline{\rho}\overline{\sigma}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\rho}(w)\overline{\sigma}(w)-\overline{\rho}(ws_{\alpha})\overline{\sigma}(ws_{\alpha}) \displaystyle=\overline{\rho}(w)\overline{\sigma}(w)-\overline{\rho}(w)\overline{\sigma}(ws_{\alpha})+\overline{\rho}(w)\overline{\sigma}(ws_{\alpha})-\overline{\rho}(ws_{\alpha})\overline{\sigma}(ws_{\alpha}) \displaystyle=\overline{\rho}(w)\left(\overline{\sigma}(w)-\overline{\sigma}(ws_{\alpha})\right)+\overline{\sigma}(ws_{\alpha})\left(\overline{\rho}(w)-\overline{\rho}(ws_{\alpha})\right), $$

and since $\overline{\rho},\overline{\sigma}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ , this lies in $\left\langle t_{w(\alpha)}\right\rangle$ . ∎

#### Lemma 2.15.

The ring $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is graded by degree.

#### Proof.

Each label given by $\mathcal{L}$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ . Thus each polynomial ideal in the definition of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is homogeneous, and so containment in each polynomial ideal is given individually by each graded piece. ∎

Some functions from $I_{2}(n)$ to $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ are elements of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ for all $H$ . Let

| $\overline{\mathbbold{1}}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ | be $\overline{\mathbbold{1}}(w)\coloneqq 1$ | for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , |
|---|---|---|
| $\overline{x}_{l}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ | be $\overline{x}_{l}(w)\coloneqq x$ | for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , |
| $\overline{y}_{l}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ | be $\overline{y}_{l}(w)\coloneqq y$ | for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , |
| $\overline{x}_{r}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ | be $\overline{x}_{r}(w)\coloneqq w(x)$ | for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , and |
| $\overline{y}_{r}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ | be $\overline{y}_{r}(w)\coloneqq w(y)$ | for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . |

Checking that $\overline{\mathbbold{1}}$ , $\overline{x}_{l}$ , and $\overline{y}_{l}$ are splines is trivial, as they are each examples of constant splines. As for $\overline{x}_{r}$ and $\overline{y}_{r}$ , we can check that

$$ \overline{x}_{r}(w)-\overline{x}_{r}(ws_{\alpha})=w(x)-ws_{\alpha}(x)=w(x-s_{\alpha}(x)). $$

Since $t_{\alpha}$ divides $x-s_{\alpha}(x)$ by Lemma 2.2, $t_{w(\alpha)}$ divides $w(x-s_{\alpha}(x))$ . The same occurs for $\overline{y}_{r}$ , and in fact these are special cases of the spline which evaluates to $w(p)$ for a fixed $p\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ .

The ring $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is an infinite-dimensional $\mathbb{C}$ -vector space in the natural way, and can also be viewed as a finitely generated graded $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module in two ways via the following module actions:

$$ f\left(x,y\right).\overline{\rho}=f\left(\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right)\overline{\rho} $$

and

$$ f\left(x,y\right).\overline{\rho}=f\left(\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right)\overline{\rho}, $$

where the right-hand side of both (4) and (5) work by substituting splines for variables into the polynomial $f$ , and then multiplying as in the ring structure of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . For both actions of the polynomial $f(x,y)$ , the constant $c=f(0,0)$ is naturally mapped to $c\overline{\mathbbold{1}}$ . Since $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is a $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -submodule of the free module $\prod_{w\in I_{2}(n)}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ for either module action, it is finitely generated. We call the module action (4) the left action and the module action (5) the right action of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ on $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . Both the left and right actions are naturally compatible with the grading on $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ .

#### Lemma 2.16.

Any minimal homogeneous (module) generating set for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ has the same number of elements in each degree.

#### Proof.

This is a straightforward consequence of the graded Nakayama Lemma [15]. One may also use the quotient defined at the end of the section to prove this directly, as in [27, Lemma 3.1]. Additionally, we will show later that this module is a free module, from which this also follows directly. ∎

So even if $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is not a free module over $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ , we can speak meaningfully about its rank-generating function. That being said, by Theorem 4.5 below, $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is in fact a free module for all $H$ , and has a very particular type of basis.

#### Definition 2.17.

Given a labeled graph $\mathcal{G}$ endowed with a partial order $\preceq$ on its vertices, a spline $\overline{\rho}$ on $\mathcal{G}$ is upper triangular from $w\in\mathcal{G}$ if $w$ is in the support of $\overline{\rho}$ and $\overline{\rho}(v)=0$ whenever $w\not\preceq v$ . In other words, $\overline{\rho}$ is supported at $w$ and only elements above $w$ .

A set $\{\overline{\rho}_{w}\mid w\in\mathcal{G}\}$ of splines on $\mathcal{G}$ is poset upper-triangular if each $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is upper triangular from $w$ .

#### Remark 2.18.

If one takes a linear extension of the poset and writes each spline $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ in a poset upper-triangular set as the rows in a matrix ordered by that linear extension, then the resulting matrix is an upper-triangular matrix.

The following is a well-known property for splines in several settings, and is a consequence of Proposition 2.6 in [20]. We include a proof for completeness.

#### Lemma 2.19.

Let $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ be a Hessenberg space. If $R=\{\overline{\rho}_{w}\mid w\in I_{2}(n)\}$ is

- (1) poset upper-triangular with respect to Bruhat order, and

- (2) $\deg(\overline{\rho}_{w})=\ell_{H}(w)$ for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ ,

then for both the left and right actions, $R$ is a minimal module generating set for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . Moreover, $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is free with $R$ as a basis, and the rank polynomial is $\displaystyle\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell_{H}(w)}$ .

#### Proof.

First we prove linear independence. Suppose $\sum_{w}f_{w}\overline{\rho}_{w}=0$ , with $f_{w}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ , and choose $w$ minimal in Bruhat order among those with $f_{w}\neq 0$ . Evaluating at $w$ , every term except $f_{w}\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)$ vanishes. Indeed, if $v<w$ , then $f_{v}=0$ by minimality, while if $v\nleq w$ , then $\overline{\rho}_{v}(w)=0$ by assumption. Thus $f_{w}\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)=0$ . Since $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is a domain and $\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)\neq 0$ , this forces $f_{w}=0$ , a contradiction. For the right action, evaluation at $w$ instead gives $w(f_{w})\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)=0$ ; since $w$ acts on $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by an automorphism, this likewise forces $f_{w}=0$ .

Now let $\overline{\rho}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . We express $\overline{\rho}$ as a $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -linear combination of the $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ by induction along a linear extension of Bruhat order, from smaller elements to larger elements. At the step indexed by $w$ , assume that the current residual spline vanishes at every $v<w$ . For each $\gamma\in H$ , the graph $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ contains the edge $(w,ws_{\gamma})$ with label $t_{w(\gamma)}$ . If $ws_{\gamma}<w$ , the spline condition gives $t_{w(\gamma)}\mid\overline{\rho}(w)$ . The forms $t_{w(\gamma)}$ , for $\gamma\in H$ , are pairwise relatively prime, so $\prod_{\gamma\in\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)}t_{w(\gamma)}$ divides $\overline{\rho}(w)$ . The same argument applies to $\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)$ , and since this is also the same degree as $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ , this product is a constant multiple of $\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)$ . Hence $\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)$ divides $\overline{\rho}(w)$ , so $g_{w}=\overline{\rho}(w)/\overline{\rho}_{w}(w)$ lies in $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ .

Replace the current residual spline $\overline{\rho}$ by $\overline{\rho}-g_{w}\overline{\rho}_{w}$ for the left action or $\overline{\rho}-w^{-1}(g_{w})\overline{\rho}_{w}$ for the right action. The new residual vanishes at $w$ . It also still vanishes at every $v<w$ , because $\overline{\rho}_{w}(v)=0$ unless $w\leq v$ . Continuing through the finite poset expresses the original spline as a $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -linear combination of $R$ .

The rank-polynomial calculation follows directly from the degree of each spline in $R$ . ∎

#### Definition 2.20.

A basis of splines satisfying the conditions in Lemma 2.19 is called a flow-up basis. The elements of such a basis are called flow-up splines. If $w$ is the minimal element in the support of a flow-up spline, then we call it a flow-up spline at $w$ .

Furthermore, $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ has the structure of an $I_{2}(n)$ -module. This was defined for the symmetric group by Tymoczko in [37].

#### Definition 2.21.

Let $\overline{\rho}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . The dot action of $I_{2}(n)$ on $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is given by

$$ (w\cdot\overline{\rho})(v)\coloneqq w(\overline{\rho}(w^{-1}v)) $$

for $w,v\in I_{2}(n)$ .

#### Lemma 2.22.

If $\overline{\rho}$ is a spline in $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ then $w\cdot\overline{\rho}$ is as well. In other words, the dot action is well-defined.

#### Proof.

For all $(v,vs_{\alpha})\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(w\cdot\overline{\rho})(v)-(w\cdot\overline{\rho})(vs_{\alpha}) \displaystyle=w\overline{\rho}(w^{-1}v)-w\overline{\rho}(w^{-1}vs_{\alpha}) \displaystyle=w(\overline{\rho}(w^{-1}v)-\overline{\rho}(w^{-1}vs_{\alpha})) \displaystyle\in w\left\langle t_{w^{-1}v(\alpha)}\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle t_{v(\alpha)}\right\rangle\qed. $$

Finally, consider the irrelevant ideal $J=\left\langle x,y\right\rangle\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . The submodule $J\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is homogeneous and $I_{2}(n)$ -equivariant. So

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\left(\mathrm{L}_{H}\right)_{i}\coloneqq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle}$}}} $$

with the left action and

$$ \mathrm{R}_{H}=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\left(\mathrm{R}_{H}\right)_{i}\coloneqq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{J\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}}}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle}$}}} $$

with the right action are each graded $\mathbb{C}[x,y]/J\cong\mathbb{C}$ -vector spaces. Since $J\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is $I_{2}(n)$ -equivariant, each of these vector spaces carries an $I_{2}(n)$ representation given by $w.[\overline{\rho}]=[w\cdot\overline{\rho}]$ . This representation is different with respect to the left and right module action. This is relatively easy to see in an example, as $\overline{x}_{l}\sim 0$ in the quotient under the left action but not the right, but $\overline{x}_{r}\sim 0$ in the quotient under the right action but not the left. The dot action fixes $\overline{x}_{r}$ but does not fix $\overline{x}_{l}$ , and so the left and right quotients interact differently with the dot action.

## 3. The Schubert case

In this section we specialize to the full reflection graph, so $H=\Phi^{+}$ . The goal is to construct a Schubert basis for $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ , prove a Borel presentation for this spline module, and then use that presentation to identify the left and right quotient representations. We define the Schubert splines using divided differences, prove their flow-up triangularity directly from the rank-two Bruhat order, and then derive the basis theorem by triangular elimination.

The defining spline condition was stated using right reflection edges. For the Schubert construction it is more convenient to use left reflection edges. The following lemma records that, in the full graph, these two descriptions are equivalent; the only difference is a possible sign in the edge label, which does not change the corresponding principal ideal.

#### Lemma 3.1.

For purposes of the spline conditions, the full reflection graph may be read using left reflection edges $w\leftrightarrow s_{\alpha}w$ , with label $t_{\alpha}$ . Equivalently,

$$ \mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}=\left\{\overline{\rho}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\middle|\allowbreak\mathchoice{\;}{\;}{\,}{\,}\mathopen{}\overline{\rho}(w)-\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}w)\in\left\langle t_{\alpha}\right\rangle\text{ for all }w\in I_{2}(n),\ \alpha\in\Phi^{+}\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

The right-hand side of (8) uses left reflection edges. We compare these with the right reflection edges in the definition of $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ .

Fix $w\in I_{2}(n)$ and $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}$ . Choose the positive root $\beta$ such that $w(\beta)=\pm\alpha$ . Since reflections depend only on the root line, $s_{\alpha}w=ws_{\beta}$ . Thus the left edge $w\leftrightarrow s_{\alpha}w$ is the same unoriented edge as the right edge $w\leftrightarrow ws_{\beta}$ . The label on this right edge is $t_{w(\beta)}=\pm t_{\alpha}$ , so it generates the same ideal as $t_{\alpha}$ . Hence the right-edge spline condition for $w\leftrightarrow ws_{\beta}$ is exactly the left-edge condition $\overline{\rho}(w)-\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}w)\in\left\langle t_{\alpha}\right\rangle$ .

The same argument also converts every right reflection edge into a left reflection edge with the same label up to sign. Therefore the two collections of divisibility conditions are identical. ∎

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $\overline{\rho}\in\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ and let $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}$ . Define

$$ \partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)\coloneq\frac{\overline{\rho}(v)-s_{\alpha}\bigl(\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)\bigr)}{t_{\alpha}}. $$

Then $\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}\in\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ .

#### Proof.

This operation is called the divided difference operator and is well known to preserve $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ for $I_{2}(n)$ and other finite Coxeter groups (including Weyl groups). We prove a slightly more general version of this in Lemma 4.1. ∎

We now define the Schubert splines. Set $\overline{\sigma}_{e}=\overline{\mathbbold{1}}$ . At the top of Bruhat order, set

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{w_{0}}(v)\coloneq\begin{cases}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}}t_{\alpha},&if $v=w_{0}$,\\
0,&otherwise.\end{cases} $$

This is a spline: all edge differences away from $w_{0}$ are zero, and every edge incident to $w_{0}$ has label $t_{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}$ , which divides the product in (10).

For $w\notin\{e,w_{0}\}$ , let $\alpha\in\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}$ be the unique simple root such that $\ell(s_{\alpha}w)=\ell(w)+1$ , whose existence and uniqueness are given by Lemma 2.4(1), and define

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{w}\coloneq\partial_{\alpha}\bigl(\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}\bigr). $$

This is a downward recursion from $w_{0}$ for all elements except $e$ . The identity class is defined separately as the constant spline, so no well-definedness issue arises at the bottom rank. By Lemma 3.2, every $\overline{\sigma}_{w}$ is a spline. The operator in (9) lowers polynomial degree by one, so the recursion is compatible with the expected grading; the next proposition proves the nonvanishing and triangularity needed for the basis theorem.

#### Proposition 3.3.

For every $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , the spline $\overline{\sigma}_{w}$ is homogeneous of degree $\ell(w)$ . It is supported on the Bruhat upper order ideal of $w$ , and its diagonal value is

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{w}(w)=\prod_{\alpha\in N_{L}(w)}t_{\alpha}. $$

Equivalently, $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v)=0$ unless $w\leq v$ .

#### Proof.

The case $w=e$ is immediate. For the remaining elements, we prove the result by downward induction on $\ell(w)$ . The base case $w=w_{0}$ is immediate: the support and degree follow from (10), and $N_{L}(w_{0})=\Phi^{+}$ .

Now let $w\notin\{e,w_{0}\}$ , and let $\alpha\in\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}$ be the unique simple root such that $\ell(s_{\alpha}w)=\ell(w)+1$ , as in Lemma 2.4(1). The recursion gives $\overline{\sigma}_{w}=\partial_{\alpha}(\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w})$ , so homogeneity follows from the induction hypothesis because the divided-difference operator lowers polynomial degree by one.

We next prove the support statement. Let $v\in I_{2}(n)$ and suppose $w\nleq v$ . Since $0<\ell(w)<n$ , Lemma 2.4(2) shows that either $\ell(v)<\ell(w)$ , or $\ell(v)=\ell(w)$ and $v\neq w$ .

If $\ell(v)<\ell(w)$ , then $s_{\alpha}w\nleq v$ and $s_{\alpha}w\nleq s_{\alpha}v$ , since $\ell(s_{\alpha}v)\leq\ell(w)<\ell(s_{\alpha}w)$ . If $\ell(v)=\ell(w)$ and $v\neq w$ , then again $s_{\alpha}w\nleq v$ . Also $s_{\alpha}w\nleq s_{\alpha}v$ . Indeed, if $\ell(s_{\alpha}v)<\ell(s_{\alpha}w)$ , this follows because Bruhat order is graded by length. If $\ell(s_{\alpha}v)=\ell(s_{\alpha}w)$ , then any comparability would force equality, and $s_{\alpha}v=s_{\alpha}w$ would force $v=w$ , contrary to the case assumption. Thus in all cases $s_{\alpha}w\nleq v$ and $s_{\alpha}w\nleq s_{\alpha}v$ . Since $\ell(s_{\alpha}w)=\ell(w)+1$ , the induction hypothesis applies to $\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}$ , and gives $\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}(v)=\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}(s_{\alpha}v)=0$ . Since $\overline{\sigma}_{w}=\partial_{\alpha}(\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w})$ , the definition of the divided-difference operator in (9) gives $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v)=0$ .

It remains to compute the diagonal value. Since $s_{\alpha}w\nleq w$ , the support statement for $\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}$ gives $\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}(w)=0$ . Hence

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{w}(w)=-\frac{s_{\alpha}(\overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}(s_{\alpha}w))}{t_{\alpha}}. $$

By the induction hypothesis and Lemma 2.4(3),

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{s_{\alpha}w}(s_{\alpha}w)=t_{\alpha}\prod_{\beta\in N_{L}(w)}t_{s_{\alpha}\beta}. $$

Applying $s_{\alpha}$ gives $-t_{\alpha}\prod_{\beta\in N_{L}(w)}t_{\beta}$ , and division by $-t_{\alpha}$ proves (12). ∎

The Schubert splines for $I_{2}(n)$ have a particularly nice formula that, for geometric cases, is a consequence of a geometric condition called rational smoothness. This is distinct from Billey’s formula for Schubert splines, which is a sum over reduced subwords of a fixed reduced expression [8]. The following is easily obtained by the same logic that appears in [10, 31, 16] in much greater generality, and agrees with the geometric cases in full Kac-Moody generality [25], but could also be proven using our Corollary 5.2 and has an even easier direct proof, which we include here.

#### Theorem 3.4.

The Schubert splines are given explicitly by

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{w}(v)=c^{w}(v)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{\gamma}v<v\\
s_{\gamma}v\not\geq w\end{subarray}}t_{\gamma} $$

where $c^{w}(v)\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$ if $w\leq v$ and $c^{w}(v)=0$ otherwise.

#### Proof.

The cases $w=e$ and $w=w_{0}$ follow from the nonzero constant spline and the top Schubert spline, respectively. Assume $0<\ell(w)<n$ . By Proposition 3.3, $\overline{\sigma}_{w}$ has degree $\ell(w)$ , its support is contained in the upper order ideal generated by $w$ , and $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(w)\neq 0$ . In the strong Bruhat graph $\mathcal{G}_{\Phi^{+}}$ , the pair $(w,v)$ is an edge whenever $\left\lvert\ell(w)-\ell(v)\right\rvert$ is an odd number (all odd-length elements of $I_{2}(n)$ are reflections). The upper order ideal $\{v\mid v\geq w\}$ contains $n-\ell(w)$ vertices of each length parity. Thus each vertex in this ideal has $n-\ell(w)$ neighbors within the ideal, out of $n$ neighbors in the full reflection graph, leaving exactly $\ell(w)$ edges to vertices outside the ideal.

Thus, the set $\{\gamma\in\Phi^{+}\mid vs_{\gamma}<v,\;vs_{\gamma}\not\geq w\}$ is size $\ell(w)$ for all $v\geq w$ . Since $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v^{\prime})=0$ for all $v^{\prime}\not\geq w$ , it follows from the divisibility conditions that, whenever $v\geq w$ ,

$$ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{\gamma}v<v\\
s_{\gamma}v\not\geq w\end{subarray}}t_{\gamma}\quad\text{divides}\quad\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v). $$

Since this product has degree $\ell(w)$ and $\overline{\sigma}_{w}$ is homogeneous of degree $\ell(w)$ , the stated formula holds with $c^{w}(v)\in\mathbb{C}$ . It remains to show that $c^{w}(v)\neq 0$ whenever $v\geq w$ .

The linear forms corresponding to distinct positive roots are pairwise non-proportional. If $v,s_{\zeta}v\geq w$ and $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v)\neq 0$ , then the edge joining these vertices lies within the upper order ideal. Therefore $t_{\zeta}$ is not proportional to any factor in either of the products

$$ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{\gamma}v<v\\
s_{\gamma}v\not\geq w\end{subarray}}t_{\gamma}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{\gamma}s_{\zeta}v<s_{\zeta}v\\
s_{\gamma}s_{\zeta}v\not\geq w\end{subarray}}t_{\gamma}. $$

Thus $t_{\zeta}$ does not divide $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v)$ . If $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(s_{\zeta}v)=0$ , the spline condition would force $t_{\zeta}\mid\overline{\sigma}_{w}(v)$ , a contradiction. Hence $c^{w}(s_{\zeta}v)\neq 0$ as well. Starting from $\overline{\sigma}_{w}(w)\neq 0$ and using connectedness of the upper order ideal gives $c^{w}(v)\neq 0$ for every $v\geq w$ , proving the claim. ∎

#### Proposition 3.5.

The Schubert splines form a homogeneous free $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -basis of $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ , namely

$$ \mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}=\bigoplus_{w\in I_{2}(n)}\mathbb{C}[x,y]\overline{\sigma}_{w},\qquad\deg\overline{\sigma}_{w}=\ell(w). $$

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from Proposition 3.3 and Lemma 2.19. ∎

#### Corollary 3.6.

The Hilbert series of the full reflection spline module is

$$ \Hilb(\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}};q)=\frac{\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell(w)}}{(1-q)^{2}}=\frac{(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})}{(1-q)^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

By Proposition 3.5, $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ is a free $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module with one homogeneous basis element of degree $\ell(w)$ for each $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . Since $\Hilb(\mathbb{C}[x,y];q)=1/(1-q)^{2}$ , this gives

$$ \Hilb(\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}};q)=\frac{\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell(w)}}{(1-q)^{2}}. $$

In $I_{2}(n)$ , there is one element of length $0$ , one element of length $n$ , and two elements of each length $1,\ldots,n-1$ . Therefore $\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell(w)}=(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})$ . ∎

We call the basis from Proposition 3.5 the Schubert basis. The next result identifies the full reflection spline module with the usual Borel presentation.

Recall that $\overline{x}_{l}(w)=x$ and $\overline{y}_{l}(w)=y$ , while $\overline{x}_{r}(w)=w(x)$ and $\overline{y}_{r}(w)=w(y)$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.

The map

$$ \Psi\colon\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}},\qquad\Psi(f\otimes h)(w)=f\,w(h), $$

is an isomorphism of graded $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -algebras, where $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ acts on the source through the first tensor factor and on $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ by the left module structure. Under this isomorphism, $x\otimes 1$ and $y\otimes 1$ correspond to $\overline{x}_{l}$ and $\overline{y}_{l}$ , while $1\otimes x$ and $1\otimes y$ correspond to $\overline{x}_{r}$ and $\overline{y}_{r}$ . Moreover, the dot action is given by $u\cdot(f\otimes h)=u(f)\otimes h$ .

#### Proof.

The map is well-defined over $\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}$ : if $p\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}$ , then $\Psi(fp\otimes h)(w)=fp\,w(h)=f\,w(p)w(h)=\Psi(f\otimes ph)(w)$ . It is also multiplicative, since $\Psi((f\otimes h)(f^{\prime}\otimes h^{\prime}))(w)=ff^{\prime}w(hh^{\prime})=\Psi(f\otimes h)(w)\Psi(f^{\prime}\otimes h^{\prime})(w)$ .

We next check that the image consists of splines. If $w\leftrightarrow ws_{\alpha}$ is a right reflection edge, then $\Psi(f\otimes h)(w)-\Psi(f\otimes h)(ws_{\alpha})=f\,w(h-s_{\alpha}(h))$ . By Lemma 2.2, $h-s_{\alpha}(h)$ is divisible by $t_{\alpha}$ , so this difference is divisible by $t_{w(\alpha)}$ , which is the edge label up to sign.

To prove injectivity, view both sides as left $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -modules and localize at the nonzero elements of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . Since $I_{2}(n)$ is a finite reflection group, $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is free over $\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}$ [23, §3.6]. Hence $\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is torsion-free as a left $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module, so localization detects injectivity.

After localization, every edge label becomes a unit, so the localized spline module is the full product $\prod_{w\in I_{2}(n)}\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])$ . The localized source is initially $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ , but the second tensor factor also localizes to $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])$ . Indeed, if $a\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is nonzero, then $N(a)=\prod_{u\in I_{2}(n)}u(a)$ is a nonzero invariant polynomial. Since $1\otimes N(a)=N(a)\otimes 1$ is invertible after localizing the first factor, and $1\otimes N(a)=\prod_{u\in I_{2}(n)}(1\otimes u(a))$ , each factor $1\otimes u(a)$ is invertible in this commutative ring. In particular, $1\otimes a$ is invertible.

Since $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])^{I_{2}(n)}=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})$ , the localized source is

$$ \operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])\otimes_{\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])^{I_{2}(n)}}\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y]). $$

The field extension $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])/\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])^{I_{2}(n)}$ is Galois with group $I_{2}(n)$ , so the canonical map

$$ \operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])\otimes_{\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])^{I_{2}(n)}}\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y])\longrightarrow\prod_{w\in I_{2}(n)}\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[x,y]),\qquad\!\!a\otimes b\longmapsto\bigl(w\mapsto a\,w(b)\bigr), $$

is an isomorphism. Thus the localized map is injective, and therefore $\Psi$ is injective.

It remains to compare Hilbert series. By Chevalley’s theorem for finite reflection groups, $\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}$ is a polynomial ring; for $I_{2}(n)$ , its basic invariant degrees are $2$ and $n$ [23, §§3.5, 3.7, Table 1]. Hence $\Hilb(\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y];q)=(1-q^{2})(1-q^{n})/(1-q)^{4}=(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})/(1-q)^{2}$ . By Corollary 3.6, this is also the Hilbert series of $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ . Since the graded pieces are finite-dimensional, the injective graded map $\Psi$ is an isomorphism.

The identifications of the coordinate splines follow directly from $\Psi(x\otimes 1)(w)=x$ , $\Psi(y\otimes 1)(w)=y$ , $\Psi(1\otimes x)(w)=w(x)$ , and $\Psi(1\otimes y)(w)=w(y)$ . Finally, for $u,v\in I_{2}(n)$ , one has $(u\cdot\Psi(f\otimes h))(v)=u(f\,(u^{-1}v)(h))=u(f)\,v(h)=\Psi(u(f)\otimes h)(v)$ , so the dot action corresponds to $u\cdot(f\otimes h)=u(f)\otimes h$ . ∎

Both submodules appearing in the quotients below are stable under the dot action: $u\cdot\overline{x}_{l}$ and $u\cdot\overline{y}_{l}$ are linear combinations of $\overline{x}_{l}$ and $\overline{y}_{l}$ , while $u\cdot\overline{x}_{r}=\overline{x}_{r}$ and $u\cdot\overline{y}_{r}=\overline{y}_{r}$ .

#### Proposition 3.8.

With respect to the left $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module structure on $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ , the quotient representation

$$ \mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}\coloneq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}} $$

is a direct sum of trivial representations, with one copy in degree $\ell(w)$ for each $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . Equivalently,

$$ \mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}\cong\bigoplus_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell(w)}\mathbbold{1} $$

as a graded $I_{2}(n)$ -representation. Hence

$$ \mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}\cong(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})\mathbbold{1}. $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.7, quotienting by $\left\langle\overline{x}_{l},\overline{y}_{l}\right\rangle$ corresponds to quotienting $\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by $\left\langle x\otimes 1,y\otimes 1\right\rangle$ . Hence

$$ \mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}\cong\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y], $$

where $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{C}[x,y]/\left\langle x,y\right\rangle$ . Since the dot action on $\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ acts only on the first tensor factor, and that factor has been quotiented to constants, the dot action on $\mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}$ is trivial.

The grading is determined by Proposition 3.5: since $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ is free over the left copy of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ with homogeneous basis $\{\overline{\sigma}_{w}\}_{w\in I_{2}(n)}$ , the classes $[\overline{\sigma}_{w}]$ form a homogeneous vector-space basis for $\mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}$ , with $\deg\overline{\sigma}_{w}=\ell(w)$ . Thus there is one copy of the trivial representation in degree $\ell(w)$ for each $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . Since $\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell(w)}=(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})$ , the claimed graded character follows. ∎

#### Proposition 3.9.

With respect to the right $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module structure on $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}$ , the quotient representation

$$ \mathrm{R}_{\Phi^{+}}\coloneq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}}$}}} $$

is isomorphic, as a graded $I_{2}(n)$ -representation, to the coinvariant algebra

$$ {\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-4.68945pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-4.43945pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{2.625pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{1.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}}. $$

In particular, since the action on $\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{1}$ is $V_{1}$ ,

$$ \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(g\mid\mathrm{R}_{\Phi^{+}};q\bigr)=\frac{(1-q^{2})(1-q^{n})}{\det(I-qV_{1}(g))} $$

for every $g\in I_{2}(n)$ . Setting $g=e$ gives

$$ \dim_{q}\mathrm{R}_{\Phi^{+}}=\frac{(1-q^{2})(1-q^{n})}{(1-q)^{2}}=(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}). $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.7, quotienting by $\left\langle\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}\right\rangle$ corresponds to quotienting $\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by $\left\langle 1\otimes x,1\otimes y\right\rangle$ . Hence

$$ \mathrm{R}_{\Phi^{+}}\cong\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}\cong{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-4.68945pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-4.43945pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{2.625pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{1.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle(\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)})_{+}\right\rangle}$}}}, $$

where $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{C}[x,y]/\left\langle x,y\right\rangle$ . Since the dot action on $\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is $u\cdot(f\otimes h)=u(f)\otimes h$ , the induced action on this quotient is the usual action of $I_{2}(n)$ on the coinvariant algebra.

By Chevalley’s theorem for finite reflection groups, $\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}$ is a polynomial ring; its basic invariant degrees are $2$ and $n$ [23, §§3.5, 3.7, Table 1]. Thus $\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}\cong\mathbb{C}[F_{2},F_{n}]$ , with $\deg F_{2}=2$ and $\deg F_{n}=n$ . Since $F_{2},F_{n}$ form a homogeneous regular sequence and are fixed by $I_{2}(n)$ , quotienting by them multiplies the graded character of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by $(1-q^{2})(1-q^{n})$ . The graded character of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is $1/\det(I-qV_{1}(g))$ , so

$$ \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(g\mid\mathrm{R}_{\Phi^{+}};q\bigr)=\frac{(1-q^{2})(1-q^{n})}{\det(I-qV_{1}(g))}. $$

The Hilbert series follows by setting $g=e$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.10.

These two quotients have the same Hilbert series, and indeed the same underlying graded vector-space type, but different $I_{2}(n)$ -actions. The dot action acts on the first tensor factor in $\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{I_{2}(n)}}\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . Therefore the left quotient kills the factor on which $I_{2}(n)$ acts, giving a trivial representation, while the right quotient kills the other factor, leaving the usual coinvariant representation.

#### Remark 3.11.

The elementary construction above is the rank-two $I_{2}(n)$ specialization of Kaji’s finite-Coxeter equivariant Schubert calculus. Kaji denotes the double coinvariant presentation by $R_{W}[t;x]$ [24, Proposition 4.1]; the equivariant Schubert classes form a free $R[t]$ -basis of this ring [24, Theorem 4.5]. Kaji also defines the finite-Coxeter GKM ring [24, Definition 4.7] and proves that the localization map identifies it with $R_{W}[t;x]$ [24, Corollary 4.10]. In this rank-two setting, we give an elementary proof using the Bruhat order, spline divisibility conditions, and basic invariant theory.

## 4. Divided Differences and Flow-up Bases

Throughout this section, all module generators, bases, and freeness statements for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ hold equally for both the left $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module structure defined in (4) and the right $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -action structure defined in (5). We consider an arbitrary Hessenberg space $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ , and show $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ has a flow-up basis (Definition 2.20) using a combination of the divided difference, the dot action, and Schubert splines.

#### Lemma 4.1.

Fix a Hessenberg space $H$ , a spline $\overline{\rho}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ , and $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}$ . If $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for all $v\in\mathrm{supp}(\overline{\rho})$ , then

$$ \partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}\coloneqq\frac{\overline{\rho}-s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}}{t_{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}. $$

#### Proof.

First we check that $\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}$ is polynomial-valued at an arbitrary $v$ . If neither $v$ nor $s_{\alpha}v$ are in the support, then divisibility holds immediately (the evaluation is $0$ ). By assumption, if either $v$ or $s_{\alpha}v$ are in the support of $\overline{\rho}$ , then $\overline{\rho}(v)-\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)$ is divisible by $t_{\alpha}$ . Also $\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)-s_{\alpha}(\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v))$ is divisible by $t_{\alpha}$ by Lemma 2.2. Hence the numerator in (14) evaluated at $v$ , which can be written as

$$ \overline{\rho}(v)-\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)+\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)-s_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v), $$

is divisible by $t_{\alpha}$ .

It remains to check the spline condition. Fix $\beta\in H$ and $v\in I_{2}(n)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)-\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(vs_{\beta}) \displaystyle=\frac{\overline{\rho}(v)-s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(v)-\overline{\rho}(vs_{\beta})+s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(vs_{\beta})}{t_{\alpha}} \displaystyle=\frac{\left(\overline{\rho}(v)-\overline{\rho}(vs_{\beta})\right)-\left(s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(v)-s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(vs_{\beta})\right)}{t_{\alpha}}. $$

Both $\overline{\rho}$ and $s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}$ are splines, the latter by Lemma 2.22. Hence the numerator is divisible by $v(t_{\beta})=t_{v(\beta)}$ .

Now if $\alpha\neq\pm v(\beta)$ , the linear forms $t_{\alpha}$ and $t_{v(\beta)}$ are relatively prime in $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . Thus the numerator is divisible by $t_{\alpha}t_{v(\beta)}$ , and after dividing by $t_{\alpha}$ we get $\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)-\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(vs_{\beta})\in\left\langle t_{v(\beta)}\right\rangle$ .

It remains only to handle $v(\beta)=\pm\alpha$ , wherein $vs_{\beta}=s_{\alpha}v$ and the edge in question is $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ . Since $s_{\alpha}(t_{\alpha})=-t_{\alpha}$ , equation (14) gives

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v) \displaystyle=\frac{\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)-s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)}{t_{\alpha}} \displaystyle=\frac{\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)-s_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)}{t_{\alpha}} \displaystyle=\frac{s_{\alpha}\left(s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(v)-\overline{\rho}(v)\right)}{t_{\alpha}} \displaystyle=s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}(v)-\overline{\rho}(v)}{-t_{\alpha}}\right) \displaystyle=s_{\alpha}(\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)). $$

Hence $\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)-\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(s_{\alpha}v)=\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v)-s_{\alpha}(\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}(v))$ , which is divisible by $t_{\alpha}$ by Lemma 2.2. ∎

#### Lemma 4.2.

Let $\alpha$ be a simple root, $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , and $\gamma$ the root such that $w<s_{\alpha}w=ws_{\gamma}$ . Then

$$ \ell(s_{\gamma})=\begin{cases}2\ell(w)+1&\text{if }2\ell(w)+1\leq n\\
2(n-\ell(w))-1&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

If on the other hand $w>s_{\alpha}w=ws_{\gamma}$ , then

$$ \ell(s_{\gamma})=\begin{cases}2\ell(w)-1&\text{if }2\ell(w)-1\leq n\\
2(n-\ell(w))+1&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

Let $\beta$ be the other simple root. Let $w<s_{\alpha}w$ so that a reduced word for $w$ is $w=s_{\beta}s_{\alpha}\cdots s_{r}$ for $r\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$ .

The first case is straightforward, as

$$ s_{\gamma}=s_{r}\cdots s_{\alpha}s_{\beta}(s_{\alpha})s_{\beta}s_{\alpha}\cdots s_{r} $$

is a reduced word if and only if its length is at most $n=\ell(w_{0})$ . If $2\ell(w)+1>n$ , then the above expression for $s_{\gamma}$ can be expressed as $w_{0}u$ with $\ell(u)=2\ell(w)+1-n$ . As $\ell(w)<n$ it follows that $\ell(u)<n$ , thus $\ell(s_{\gamma})=n-\ell(u)=2(n-\ell(w))-1$ .

The result for $w>s_{\alpha}w$ can be achieved by replacing $\ell(w)$ with $\ell(s_{\alpha}w)=\ell(w)-1$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.3.

Consider $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , a simple root $\alpha$ , and say that $w<s_{\alpha}w$ . Let $H$ be a Hessenberg space. The following hold.

- (1) If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\notin\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , then $\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)=\mathrm{inv}_{H}(s_{\alpha}w)$ .

- (2) If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , then $\ell_{H}(w)+1=\ell_{H}(s_{\alpha}w)$ .

- (3) If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , then one of the following holds: • $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for every $v$ with $\ell(v)\leq\ell(w)$ , occurring when $2\ell(w)+1\leq n$ , or • $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for every $v$ with $\ell(v)>\ell(w)$ otherwise.

- (4) If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ where $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for all $v$ where $\ell(v)\leq\ell(w)$ and $2\ell(w)+1\leq n$ , then $\ell_{H}(w)=\ell(w)$ .

#### Proof.

(1) Since $w<s_{\alpha}w$ , we know that $\alpha$ is a left descent of $s_{\alpha}w$ . Since $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\notin\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , we know that $w^{-1}(\alpha)\notin H$ . Recall that $N_{R}(w)$ is the set of right inversions of $w$ , and $N_{R}(s_{\alpha}w)=N_{R}(w)\cup\{w^{-1}(\alpha)\}$ by Lemma 2.4, and so the intersection $N_{R}(w)\cap H=\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)$ does not change. Essentially the exact same logic applies to prove (2), where $w^{-1}(\alpha)\in H$ .

(3) If $s_{\alpha}w=ws_{\gamma}$ , then $s_{\gamma}=w^{-1}s_{\alpha}w$ . By Lemma 4.2

$$ \ell(s_{\gamma})=\begin{cases}2\ell(w)+1&\text{if }2\ell(w)+1\leq n\\
2(n-\ell(w))-1&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Since $H$ is a lower order ideal for $I_{2}(n)$ , $\gamma\in H$ implies $\gamma^{\prime}\in H$ for all $\gamma^{\prime}$ such that $\ell(s_{\gamma^{\prime}})<\ell(s_{\gamma})$ . Assume first that $\ell(s_{\gamma})=2\ell(w)+1$ . If $\ell(v)\leq\ell(w)$ then

$$ \ell(v^{-1}s_{\alpha}v)\leq 2\ell(v)+1\leq 2\ell(w)+1\leq n. $$

Thus $\ell(v^{-1}s_{\alpha}v)=2\ell(v)\pm 1\leq\ell(s_{\gamma})$ , with equality only when $v=w$ , and so $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ .

Now assume $2\ell(w)+1>n$ and consider all $v$ where $\ell(v)>\ell(w)$ . If $\ell(v)\geq\ell(w)+2$ then

$$ \ell(v^{-1}s_{\alpha}v)=2(n-\ell(v))\pm 1<2(n-\ell(w))-1=\ell(s_{\gamma}). $$

If $\ell(v)=\ell(w)+1$ , there are two options. Either $v=s_{\alpha}w$ , in which case $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ by assumption. If $v\neq s_{\alpha}w$ is the other element of length $\ell(w)+1$ , then $v<s_{\alpha}v$ , in which case $\ell(v^{-1}s_{\alpha}v)=2(n-\ell(v))-1$ and the required inequality holds.

(4) This also leverages Lemma 4.2. If $\zeta\in N_{L}(w)$ and $\gamma\in\Phi^{+}$ is such that $s_{\zeta}w=ws_{\gamma}$ , then

$$ \ell(s_{\gamma})=\ell(w^{-1}s_{\zeta}w)\leq\ell(w^{-1})+\ell(s_{\zeta}w)<2\ell(w)<\ell(w^{-1}s_{\alpha}w), $$

and so $\gamma\in H$ and $(w,s_{\zeta}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ . Thus $N_{R}(w)\subseteq H$ , so $\ell_{H}(w)=\left\lvert N_{R}(w)\right\rvert=\ell(w)$ . ∎

#### Corollary 4.4.

Let $H$ be a Hessenberg space. If $w\in I_{2}(n)$ with $2\ell(w)+1>n$ , $\alpha$ is a simple root such that $w<s_{\alpha}w$ and $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for all $v\geq w$ , then there exists a flow-up spline at $w$ .

#### Proof.

We can assume that $w\notin\{e,w_{0}\}$ . Consider an arbitrary $v\in I_{2}(n)$ such that $w\leq v<w_{0}$ . We first show that if $s_{\gamma}$ is the left-ascent of $v$ with $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$ , then $(v,s_{\gamma}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ . If $\gamma=\alpha$ , then the edge $(v,s_{\gamma}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ by assumption.

If $s_{\beta}v>v$ , then $v\neq w$ . In particular, $\ell(v)>\ell(w)$ , so Lemma 4.2 gives us that $\ell(v^{-1}s_{\beta}v)$ is strictly less than $\ell(w^{-1}s_{\alpha}w)$ . So if $s_{\beta}v=vs_{\zeta}$ and $s_{\alpha}w=ws_{\nu}$ , it follows that $\ell(s_{\zeta})<\ell(s_{\nu})$ and thus $(v,s_{\beta}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ .

So $(v,s_{\gamma}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for all $s_{\gamma}v>v\geq w$ and $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$ . We proceed by induction on $\ell(v)$ backwards from $\ell(w_{0})=n$ , where such a spline exists:

$$ \overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}(v)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\displaystyle\prod_{\alpha\in H}t_{w_{0}(\alpha)}&\text{if }v=w_{0}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Say that such a spline exists for all $v^{\prime}$ such that $\ell(v^{\prime})>\ell(v)$ . If $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$ is such that $s_{\gamma}v>v$ , our assumption guarantees that $(v,s_{\gamma}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ . Our induction assumption gives a spline $\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}$ supported at $v^{\prime}=s_{\gamma}v$ and above of degree $\ell_{H}(s_{\gamma}v)$ . If $u\in\mathrm{supp}(\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v})-\{s_{\gamma}v\}$ , then $\ell(u)>\ell(s_{\gamma}v)$ , so $\ell(u^{-1}s_{\gamma}u)<\ell(v^{-1}s_{\gamma}v)$ (even if $s_{\gamma}u<u$ ) implying $(u,s_{\gamma}u)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ . So we can apply Lemma 4.1 to get a spline $\partial_{\gamma}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}$ of degree $\ell_{H}(s_{\gamma}v)-1$ , which is precisely $\ell_{H}(v)$ by Lemma 4.3(2). This spline $\partial_{\gamma}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}$ is nonzero at $v$ since

$$ \partial_{\gamma}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}(v)=-s_{\gamma}\bigl(\bar{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}(s_{\gamma}v)\bigr)/t_{\gamma}\neq 0. $$

By assumption, $\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}$ is supported only at $s_{\gamma}v$ and above. If $u\geq s_{\gamma}v$ and $u\neq s_{\gamma}v$ , then $\ell(s_{\gamma}u)\geq\ell(v)+1$ , so $s_{\gamma}u\geq v$ by Lemma 2.4(2), and thus $s_{\gamma}\cdot\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}$ is also supported only at $v$ and above. Therefore, the spline $\partial_{\gamma}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\gamma}v}$ is supported only at $v$ and above. The induction argument terminates at $v=w$ and $\gamma=\alpha$ , and we have the claim. ∎

#### Theorem 4.5.

Fix a Hessenberg space $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ . Then $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ has a flow-up basis $\{\overline{\rho}_{w}\mid w\in I_{2}(n)\}$ , given by

$$ \overline{\rho}_{w}=\begin{cases}\overline{\mathbbold{1}}&\text{if }w=e\\
\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}\text{ from }\eqref{eq:top_spline}&\text{if }w=w_{0}\\
\overline{\sigma}_{w}\text{ from }\eqref{eq:schubert_recursion}&\text{if }(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}\text{ and }2\ell(w)+1\leq n,\\
\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w}&\text{if }(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}\text{ and }2\ell(w)+1>n,\\
s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w}&\text{if }(w,s_{\alpha}w)\notin\mathcal{E}_{H},\end{cases} $$

where $\alpha$ is the unique left simple ascent of $w\notin\{e,w_{0}\}$ .

#### Proof.

Consider $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . The identity spline $\overline{\mathbbold{1}}$ is a flow-up spline at $e$ and $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ as in the proof of Corollary 4.4 is a flow-up spline at $w_{0}$ . So let $w\notin\{e,w_{0}\}$ and $\alpha$ be the simple root where $s_{\alpha}w>w$ .

If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , then Lemma 4.3(3) gives $(v,s_{\alpha}v)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ for either (a) all $v$ with $\ell(v)\leq\ell(w)$ when $2\ell(w)+1\leq n$ , or (b) for all $v$ with $\ell(v)>\ell(w)$ otherwise. If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ and $2\ell(w)+1\leq n$ , then we take the Schubert spline, which has degree $\ell_{H}(w)$ by Lemma 4.3(4). If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ and $2\ell(w)+1>n$ then we have a flow-up spline at $w$ by Corollary 4.4.

If $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\notin\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , then we can proceed by downwards induction, with the assumption that a flow-up spline exists at all $v>w$ . In particular, there is a flow-up spline at $s_{\alpha}w$ . Let $\overline{\rho}$ be the flow-up spline at $s_{\alpha}w$ and consider $s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}$ , which has the appropriate support since $\{s_{\alpha}v\mid v\geq s_{\alpha}w\}\subseteq\{v\mid v\geq w\}$ in strong Bruhat order when $s_{\alpha}w>w$ , and the appropriate degree by Lemma 4.3(1), and is thus a flow-up spline at $w$ . ∎

\overline{\rho}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{1}}&\text{supported weakly above}&s_{1}s_{2}s_{1}&\text{given by}&s_{2}\cdot\partial_{1}\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}\\
\overline{\rho}_{s_{2}s_{1}s_{2}}&\text{supported weakly above}&s_{2}s_{1}s_{2}&\text{given by}&\partial_{1}\partial_{2}\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}\\
\overline{\rho}_{(s_{1}s_{2})^{2}}&\text{supported weakly above}&(s_{1}s_{2})^{2}&\text{given by}&\partial_{2}\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}\\

It follows that the rank generating function for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is $1+4q+4q^{2}+q^{3}$ .
