#### Corollary 4.7.

The rank generating function for $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is palindromic and given by

$$ P_{H}(q)=\sum_{w\in I_{2}(n)}q^{\ell_{H}(w)}. $$

If $\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h$ then

$$ \displaystyle P_{H}(q) \displaystyle=\displaystyle 1+2q+\cdots+2q^{h-1}+(2n-4h+2)q^{h}+2q^{h+1}+\cdots+2q^{2h-1}+q^{2h} \displaystyle=(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{2h-1})+(2n-4h)q^{h}. $$

If $\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h+1$ then

$$ \displaystyle P_{H}(q) \displaystyle=1+2q+\cdots+2q^{h-1}+(n-2h+1)\left(q^{h}+q^{h+1}\right)+2q^{h+2}+\cdots+2q^{2h}+q^{2h+1} \displaystyle=(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{2h})+(n-2h-1)(q^{h}+q^{h+1}) $$

Furthermore, the Hilbert series of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is

$$ \Hilb(\mathcal{M}_{H};q)=\frac{P_{H}(q)}{(1-q)^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

The first formulation follows directly from Theorem 4.5. As for being palindromic, the longest element satisfies $w_{0}(\Phi^{+})=\Phi^{-}$ , so $\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w_{0}w)=H\setminus\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)$ for all $w\in I_{2}(n)$ and $w\mapsto w_{0}w$ gives an $H$ -inversion reversing involution.

Now we compute the first $h$ coefficients of $P_{H}(q)$ . Clearly $P_{H}(0)=1$ . Let $w\in I_{2}(n)$ be a non-identity element and say without loss of generality that a reduced word for $w$ ends in $s_{\alpha}$ . Then $w(s_{\alpha}s_{\beta})^{k}s_{\alpha}<w$ for all $0\leq k<\ell(w)$ . Specifically, if $\ell(w)<h$ then $\ell(w)=\ell_{H}(w)$ and if $\ell(w)\geq h$ then $\ell_{H}(w)\geq h$ . Thus the coefficient of $q^{k}$ for $k\in[h-1]$ is $2$ , the number of $w\in I_{2}(n)$ with length $k$ , and so the initial segment of $h$ coefficients is $(1,2,\ldots,2)$ . The polynomials above are the unique palindromic polynomials of degree $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ with coefficient sum $2n$ that have this initial segment of coefficients. ∎

## 5. Properties of the Flow-up Basis

This section will prove two main results. The first is a concrete description of $\overline{\rho}_{w}(v)$ for all $v$ and $w$ . The second is a linear independence result on particular orbits $I_{2}(n)\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w}$ that will be critical for our computations in Sections 6 and 7.

#### Lemma 5.1.

Consider $G=\{w,ws_{1},ws_{1}s_{2},\ldots,w(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}\}$ . If $\alpha_{2k+1}\in H$ then the subgraph of $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ induced by $G$ is regular.

Similarly, if $G=\{w,ws_{2},\ldots,w(s_{2}s_{1})^{k}s_{2}\}$ and $\alpha_{2k+2}\in H$ , then the subgraph of $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ induced by $G$ is regular.

#### Proof.

The root $\alpha_{2k+1}$ is associated to the reflection $(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}$ . If $\alpha_{2k+1}\in H$ then $\alpha_{i}\in H$ for all $i\leq 2k$ . In particular, an edge exists in $\mathcal{G}$ for right multiplication by any reflection of length at most $2k-1$ .

List the elements of $G$ as such:

$$ (v_{0},v_{1},\ldots,v_{2k+1})\coloneqq(w,ws_{1},\ldots,w(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}). $$

Then $(v_{0},v_{j})$ is an edge in $\mathcal{G}$ for every odd $j\in\{0,\ldots,2k+1\}$ . Similarly, for any even $i$ and odd $j$ in $[2k+1]$ , the pair $(v_{i},v_{j})$ is an edge in $\mathcal{G}$ via:

- • right multiplication by some $(s_{1}s_{2})^{l}s_{1}$ for $l\leq k$ if $i<j$ , or

- • right multiplication by some $(s_{2}s_{1})^{l}s_{2}$ for $l<k$ if $j<i$ .

In particular, every even-indexed $v_{i}$ in $G$ is connected to every odd-indexed $v_{j}$ in $G$ , and vice versa. Since $\{0,\ldots,2k+1\}$ has the same number of odd and even integers (and two elements in $G$ of the same parity index cannot be connected), we get that $G$ is regular.

The proof for the $G=\{w,\ldots,w(s_{2}s_{1})^{k}s_{2}\}$ is the same with slightly different indices, and in any case follows by symmetry. ∎

So the number of edges leaving $G$ in $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ is also the same for each vertex in $G$ . In particular, we get the following corollary.

#### Corollary 5.2.

Fix $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . If $\alpha_{2k+1}\in H$ then any nonzero homogeneous spline with support contained in

$$ G=\{w,ws_{1},ws_{1}s_{2},\ldots,w(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}\}, $$

respectively $\alpha_{2k+2}\in H$ and with support contained in

$$ G=\{w,ws_{2},\ldots,w(s_{2}s_{1})^{k}s_{2}\}, $$

of degree $N=\left\lvert\{\alpha\in H\mid ws_{\alpha}\notin G\}\right\rvert$ must be of the form

$$ \overline{\sigma}(v)=c^{w}(v)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in H\\
vs_{\alpha}\notin G\end{subarray}}t_{v(\alpha)} $$

where $c^{w}(v)\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$ when $v\in G$ and $\overline{\sigma}(v)=0$ otherwise. Moreover, if such a spline exists, there is a unique one normalized by $c^{w}(w)=1$ .

#### Proof.

The product $\displaystyle\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in H\\ vs_{\alpha}\notin G\end{subarray}}t_{v(\alpha)}$ divides $\overline{\sigma}(v)$ , as each $v(\alpha)$ is a pairwise non-proportional linear form and $\overline{\sigma}(vs_{\alpha})=0$ when $vs_{\alpha}\notin G$ by assumption. Lemma 5.1 ensures that this product is degree $N$ . As such, we get the above form for $c^{w}(v)\in\mathbb{C}$ and it remains to prove that $c^{w}(v)\neq 0$ for all $v\in G$ .

Since $\overline{\sigma}\neq 0$ , certainly $c^{w}(v)\neq 0$ for some $v\in G$ . If $v_{1},v_{2}\in G$ are connected by an edge in $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ labeled by $\beta$ and $c^{w}(v_{1})\neq 0$ , then $t_{\beta}$ cannot appear in the products for $\overline{\sigma}(v_{1})$ or $\overline{\sigma}(v_{2})$ . Since these roots are pairwise non-proportional, $t_{\beta}$ does not divide $\overline{\sigma}(v_{1})$ . If $c^{w}(v_{2})=0$ , then $\overline{\sigma}(v_{2})=0$ , and the spline condition would force $t_{\beta}\mid\overline{\sigma}(v_{1})$ , a contradiction. Thus $c^{w}(v_{2})\neq 0$ . Since $G$ is connected, $c^{w}(v)\neq 0$ for all $v\in G$ .

The moreover part of the proof will proceed in much the same way. Say that $c^{w}(v_{1})$ is uniquely determined from $c^{w}(w)=1$ and $v_{2}$ is adjacent to $v_{1}$ with edge label $\beta$ . Consider $\displaystyle\left[\overline{\sigma}(v_{1})\right],\left[\overline{\sigma}(v_{2})\right]\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{\left\langle t_{\beta}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\textstyle{\left\langle t_{\beta}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{2.625pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptstyle{\left\langle t_{\beta}\right\rangle}$}}{\raisebox{1.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.75pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\langle t_{\beta}\right\rangle}$}}}$ . This quotient is (non-canonically) isomorphic to the polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[t]$ . We have established that neither class is zero, and so choosing any particular graded isomorphism to $\mathbb{C}[t]$ gives $[\overline{\sigma}(v_{1})]\mapsto c^{w}(v_{1})c_{1}t^{N}$ and $[\overline{\sigma}(v_{2})]\mapsto c^{w}(v_{2})c_{2}t^{N}$ for some $c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$ . Since $[\overline{\sigma}(v_{1})-\overline{\sigma}(v_{2})]=0$ , we get that $c^{w}(v_{2})=\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}c^{w}(v_{1})$ . So we have determined the value of $c^{w}(v_{2})$ , and since $G$ is connected we have the claim. ∎

Now we turn these results towards the flow-up basis $\{\overline{\rho}_{w}\mid w\in I_{2}(n)\}$ that we have constructed with Schubert splines, the dot action, and the divided difference operator. We have now as well the tool to define their supports.

#### Proposition 5.3.

Let $w\in I_{2}(n)$ . Then either $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is a Schubert spline, $w=w_{0}$ and $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ is given, or $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ satisfies the conditions in Corollary 5.2.

#### Proof.

If $\overline{\rho}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ , then $\mathrm{supp}(v\cdot\overline{\rho})=\{vu\mid u\in\mathrm{supp}(\overline{\rho})\}$ . Furthermore, since the dot action preserves degree, we have that if $\overline{\rho}$ satisfies the conditions in Corollary 5.2 then so does $v\cdot\overline{\rho}$ for all $v\in I_{2}(n)$ .

As such, it remains to check those flow-up splines $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ that are achieved by repeatedly applying the divided difference operator to $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ . We take $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ as the base case, with its support and values given directly by (15), and proceed by induction.

Take such a $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ where $\alpha$ is a left ascent of $w$ , $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ , and $2\ell(w)+1>n$ . By Theorem 4.5, we have $\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w}=\overline{\rho}_{w}$ . Now $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is supported on the upper order ideal generated by $w$ , so we let $G=\{v\in I_{2}(n)\mid w\leq v\}$ . By Corollary 4.4, the degree of $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is $\ell_{H}(w)=\left\lvert\{\gamma\in H\mid ws_{\gamma}\notin G\}\right\rvert$ . Furthermore, if $s_{1}$ is the unique right ascent of $w$ then

$$ G=\left\{w,ws_{1},ws_{1}s_{2},\ldots,w_{0},\ldots,w(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}=s_{\alpha}w\right\}, $$

where $\alpha_{2k+1}\in H$ . If $s_{2}$ is the unique right ascent, then the same occurs with $\alpha_{2k+2}$ , and thus $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ satisfies the conditions in Corollary 5.2. ∎

When combined with Theorem 3.4, we have an explicit description of each flow-up spline $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ . The support $G_{w}$ is either the upper order ideal generated by $w$ , or the set given in Corollary 5.2.

#### Proposition 5.4.

Fix an integer $k\geq 0$ with $2k+1<n$ , and define

$$ H\coloneqq\{\gamma\in\Phi^{+}\mid\ell(s_{\gamma})\leq 2k+1\}=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2k+2}\}. $$

For each distinct set of the form

$$ G=\{w,ws_{1},\ldots,w(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}\}\qquad\text{or}\qquad G=\{w,ws_{2},\ldots,w(s_{2}s_{1})^{k}s_{2}\}, $$

choose constants $c^{G}(v)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ for $v\in G$ , and define $\overline{\sigma}_{G}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{G}(v)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle c^{G}(v)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in H\\
vs_{\alpha}\notin G\end{subarray}}t_{v(\alpha)},&v\in G,\\[6.0pt]
0,&v\notin G.\end{cases} $$

Then the set of functions $\{\overline{\sigma}_{G}\}$ for all such $G$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{C}$ .

#### Proof.

Since there are duplicates in the descriptions of $G$ , it will be convenient to choose an indexing for $I_{2}(n)$ within this proof that removes this ambiguity. Let $v_{0}=e$ , $v_{1}=s_{1}$ , and more generally

$$ \displaystyle v_{2j} \displaystyle=(s_{1}s_{2})^{j}, \displaystyle v_{2j+1} \displaystyle=(s_{1}s_{2})^{j}s_{1}, $$

up to $v_{2n-1}=s_{2}$ . Read all vertex indices modulo $2n$ . Then let

$$ G_{i}=\{v_{i},v_{i+1},\ldots,v_{i+2k+1}\}, $$

and denote $\overline{\sigma}_{G_{i}}$ by $\overline{\sigma}_{i}$ , for all $i\in\{0,\ldots,2n-1\}$ .

Consider a linear relation $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}=0$ , where $c_{i}\in\mathbb{C}$ . Since this is a linear relation of functions, we may evaluate it at any $w\in I_{2}(n)$ and it must evaluate to $0$ . In particular,

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(v_{1})=0. $$

Many of these evaluations are $0$ because $e$ or $v_{1}$ are not in the support, so we consider the subset

$$ \left\{\overline{\sigma}_{2n-2k-1},\overline{\sigma}_{2n-2k},\ldots,\overline{\sigma}_{2n-1},\overline{\sigma}_{0},\overline{\sigma}_{1}\right\} $$

whose supports contain at least one of $e$ and $v_{1}$ . Consider the sequence $S=(2n-2k-1,\ldots,2n-1,0,1)$ , so that

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)=\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(v_{1})=\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(v_{1}). $$

We will prove that $c_{i}=0$ for all $i\in S$ .

For contradiction, let $m$ be the earliest-appearing index in $S$ where $c_{m}\neq 0$ . If $m=0$ , then

$$ \sum_{i\in S}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)=c_{0}\overline{\sigma}_{0}(e)+c_{1}\overline{\sigma}_{1}(e)=c_{0}\overline{\sigma}_{0}(e)=c_{0}c^{G_{0}}(e)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in H\\
s_{\alpha}\notin G_{0}\end{subarray}}t_{\alpha}\neq 0, $$

a contradiction. Similarly, if $m=1$ , then

$$ \sum_{i\in S}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(v_{1})=c_{1}\overline{\sigma}_{1}(v_{1})\neq 0. $$

So $m\in\{2n-2k-1,\ldots,2n-1\}$ .

If $m=2n-2q-1$ for $q\in\{0,\ldots,k\}$ , then $v_{m}$ and $v_{0}$ differ by a reflection of length at most $2k+1$ . By the definition of $H$ , this reflection corresponds to a root $\gamma\in H$ . Now $v_{m}\notin G_{i}$ for all

$$ i\in J_{m}\coloneqq\{m+1,\ldots,2n-1,0,1\}, $$

so $t_{\gamma}$ divides $\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)$ for every such $i$ , whereas it does not divide $\overline{\sigma}_{m}(e)$ .

Now we consider evaluation of the polynomials themselves. Since distinct positive roots are non-proportional, any nonzero point $p_{\gamma}\in\ker t_{\gamma}$ satisfies $t_{\alpha}(p_{\gamma})\neq 0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\setminus\{\gamma\}$ . As such,

$$ \displaystyle\left[\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)\right](p_{\gamma}) \displaystyle=\left[\sum_{i\in\{m\}\cup J_{m}}c_{i}\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)\right](p_{\gamma}) \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\{m\}\cup J_{m}}c_{i}[\overline{\sigma}_{i}(e)](p_{\gamma}) \displaystyle=c_{m}[\overline{\sigma}_{m}(e)](p_{\gamma}). $$

Since $[\overline{\sigma}_{m}(e)](p_{\gamma})\neq 0$ , the relation forces $c_{m}=0$ , giving a contradiction.

If, on the other hand, $m=2n-2q$ for $q\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ , then $v_{m}$ and $v_{1}$ differ by right multiplication by a reflection of length at most $2k+1$ , so they are joined by an edge of $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ . The remaining contradiction proceeds exactly as it did for $m=2n-2q-1$ , this time evaluating the functions at $v_{1}$ and then evaluating the resulting polynomials at a nonzero point in the kernel of the label of this edge. The incident labels at $v_{1}$ are pairwise non-proportional, so the same argument applies.

Thus no such $m$ exists, and $c_{i}=0$ for all $i\in S$ . For each $j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ , left multiplication by $(s_{1}s_{2})^{-j}$ sends $v_{2j}$ to $e$ , $v_{2j+1}$ to $v_{1}$ , and $G_{i}$ to $G_{i-2j}$ , with indices read modulo $2n$ . It preserves $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ and transforms its labels by an invertible linear map. Applying the same argument at $v_{2j}$ and $v_{2j+1}$ therefore gives $c_{i+2j}=0$ for every $i\in S$ . Since $0,1\in S$ , this gives $c_{2j}=c_{2j+1}=0$ for every $j$ . Hence all coefficients vanish, proving linear independence. ∎

#### Corollary 5.5.

Let $H\subsetneq\Phi^{+}$ be a Hessenberg space with $|H|=2k+1$ . Consider the sets

$$ G=\{w,ws_{1},\ldots,w(s_{1}s_{2})^{k}s_{1}\}\qquad\text{when }\alpha_{2k+1}\in H, $$

and

$$ G=\{w,ws_{2},\ldots,w(s_{2}s_{1})^{k}s_{2}\}\qquad\text{when }\alpha_{2k+2}\in H. $$

For each distinct such $G$ , choose constants $c^{G}(v)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ for $v\in G$ , and define $\overline{\sigma}_{G}\colon I_{2}(n)\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by

$$ \overline{\sigma}_{G}(v)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle c^{G}(v)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in H\\
vs_{\gamma}\notin G\end{subarray}}t_{v(\gamma)},&v\in G,\\[6.0pt]
0,&v\notin G.\end{cases} $$

Then these functions are linearly independent over $\mathbb{C}$ .

#### Proof.

Write

$$ H^{*}=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2k+2}\}=H\cup\{\delta\}. $$

For each set $G$ under consideration, the proof of Lemma 5.1 shows that the subgraph induced by $G$ in $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ is complete bipartite, with parts given by length parity. Consequently, $vs_{\delta}\notin G$ for every $v\in G$ : otherwise $v$ and $vs_{\delta}$ would be opposite-parity vertices in $G$ whose connecting edge does not belong to $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ .

Define

$$ \overline{\tau}_{G}(v)\coloneqq t_{v(\delta)}\overline{\sigma}_{G}(v). $$

Since the $\delta$ -edge leaves $G$ at every $v\in G$ , these functions satisfy

$$ \overline{\tau}_{G}(v)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle c^{G}(v)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in H^{*}\\
vs_{\gamma}\notin G\end{subarray}}t_{v(\gamma)},&v\in G,\\[6.0pt]
0,&v\notin G.\end{cases} $$

Because $2k+1=|H|<n$ , these functions form a subfamily of the linearly independent family in Proposition 5.4, applied to $H^{*}$ .

Any relation $\sum_{G}a_{G}\overline{\sigma}_{G}=0$ , with $a_{G}\in\mathbb{C}$ , gives $\sum_{G}a_{G}\overline{\tau}_{G}=0$ after pointwise multiplication by $v\mapsto t_{v(\delta)}$ . Hence every $a_{G}$ is zero. ∎

## 6. The Left Representation

In this section, we will compute the dot action representation $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ .

For non-negative integer $h$ at most $(n-1)/2$ for $n$ odd and at most $n/2-1$ for $n$ even, set the following notation:

$$ \mathsf{P}_{h}\coloneqq\mathbbold{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{h}V_{j}. $$

#### Remark 6.1.

We record three facts about $\mathsf{P}_{h}$ . First, the dimension is $2h+1$ . Second, the virtual representation $C_{\gamma}-\mathsf{P}_{h}$ is in fact a representation for all $h$ . Finally, when $n$ is odd then $C_{\gamma}\cong\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)/2}$ , but when $n$ is even $C_{\gamma}\cong\eta_{\gamma}\oplus\mathsf{P}_{n/2-1}$ .

#### Definition 6.2.

Let $H$ be a Hessenberg space with simple roots $\alpha,\beta$ , and let $h=\lfloor\left\lvert H\right\rvert/2\rfloor$ . The simple root $\alpha$ is $H$ -dominant if there is a $w=s_{\beta}s_{\alpha}\cdots\in I_{2}(n)$ with $\ell_{H}(w)=h$ such that $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ but $(w,s_{\beta}w)\notin\mathcal{E}_{H}$ .

#### Remark 6.3.

Assume $H\subsetneq\Phi^{+}$ . When $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ is even, both simple roots satisfy the definition for $H$ -dominant. When $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ is odd, one of the simple roots will be $H$ -dominant, and for the other no such $w$ exists. The main consequence is that, in view of Theorem 6.4 below, when $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ is odd and $n$ is even, the representation $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ does in fact depend on which of the two Hessenberg spaces of size $2h+1$ are chosen to be $H$ .

#### Theorem 6.4.

Let $H\subsetneq\Phi^{+}$ be a Hessenberg space, let $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ be the simple roots, and set $h=\lfloor|H|/2\rfloor$ . If $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ is odd, let $\alpha$ be the $H$ -dominant simple root. Then, as an element of the graded representation ring of $I_{2}(n)$ ,

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}\cong\begin{cases}\displaystyle(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{2h-1})\mathbbold{1}\oplus q^{h}\left(C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1}\right),&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h,\\[10.0pt]
\displaystyle(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{2h})\mathbbold{1}\oplus(q^{h}+q^{h+1})\left(C_{\alpha}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right),&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h+1.\end{cases} $$

In particular, the graded representation $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ is palindromic.

#### Remark 6.5.

Taking dimensions in (17) recovers the rank generating function in Corollary 4.7.

#### Example 6.6.

When $H=\Phi^{+}$ , the theorem as written does not apply. Its formula extends to this case when $n$ is odd, since then $C_{\alpha}\cong\mathsf{P}_{h}$ . When $n$ is even, $h=n/2$ lies outside the defined range of $\mathsf{P}_{h}$ . In either case, the representation is

$$ \mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}\cong(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})\mathbbold{1}, $$

which is Proposition 3.8.

#### Example 6.7.

When $H=\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\}$ , one has $h=1$ , so

$$ \displaystyle C_{\alpha_{1}}\oplus C_{\alpha_{2}}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1} \displaystyle\cong C_{\alpha_{1}}\oplus C_{\alpha_{2}}-V_{1}-\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2} $$

It follows that

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}\cong\begin{cases}\displaystyle\mathbbold{1}\oplus\left(\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}\oplus V_{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=2}^{(n-1)/2}V_{j}^{\oplus 2}\right)q\oplus\mathbbold{1}q^{2}&n\text{ odd}\\
\displaystyle\mathbbold{1}\oplus\left(\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}\oplus\eta_{0}\oplus\eta_{1}\oplus V_{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=2}^{n/2-1}V_{j}^{\oplus 2}\right)q\oplus\mathbbold{1}q^{2}&n\text{ even}\end{cases} $$

#### Example 6.8.

When $H=\Phi^{+}\setminus\{\alpha_{n}\}$ and $n$ is even, it follows that $h=n/2-1$ and if $\alpha$ is the $H$ -dominant simple root then

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}\cong(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-2})\mathbbold{1}\oplus(q^{n/2-1}+q^{n/2})\eta_{\alpha}. $$

When $n$ is odd, it is the case that $h=(n-1)/2$ and

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}\cong(1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-2})\mathbbold{1}\oplus(q^{(n-1)/2})V_{(n-1)/2}. $$

The remainder of this section is dedicated to proving Theorem 6.4. The key tool is equivariant freeness. Assume throughout that $H\neq\Phi^{+}$ , since the full-reflection case has already been proved. In particular, if $\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h$ or $2h+1$ , then $h<n/2$ . Write $\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{d}$ for the homogeneous degree- $d$ piece of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ . The quotient map

$$ \mathcal{M}_{H}\longrightarrow\mathrm{L}_{H} $$

is graded and $I_{2}(n)$ -equivariant. Since $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is free over $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ by Theorem 4.5, by Maschke’s theorem we can choose a graded equivariant section of this quotient. Together with graded Nakayama, this gives a noncanonical isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{M}_{H}\cong\mathbb{C}[x,y]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathrm{L}_{H} $$

of graded $I_{2}(n)$ -representations, where $I_{2}(n)$ acts diagonally on the right-hand side. Consequently,

$$ (\mathcal{M}_{H})_{d}\cong\bigoplus_{j=0}^{d}\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{j}\otimes(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d-j}. $$

The following proposition proves that $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ is palindromic, which reduces the Theorem 6.4 to calculating $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d}$ for $d\leq h$ .

#### Proposition 6.9.

The top graded piece of $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ is the trivial representation. For every $0\leq d\leq\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ , multiplication in the graded algebra $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ restricts to a perfect $I_{2}(n)$ -invariant pairing

$$ (\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d}\otimes(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}\longrightarrow(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\cong\mathbbold{1}. $$

Consequently,

$$ (\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}\cong(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d}^{*}\cong(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d} $$

as $I_{2}(n)$ -representations.

#### Proof.

Let $\{\overline{\rho}_{w}\mid w\in I_{2}(n)\}$ be as in Theorem 4.5, so that its $w_{0}$ -element is given by (15). For each $w\in I_{2}(n)$ , define the corresponding flow-down spline by $\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{w}\coloneqq w_{0}\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}w}$ .

If $v\in\mathrm{supp}(\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{w})$ , then $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}w}(w_{0}v)\neq 0$ , and hence $w_{0}w\leq w_{0}v$ . Left multiplication by $w_{0}$ reverses Bruhat order, so $v\leq w$ . Therefore

$$ \mathrm{supp}\left(\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{w}\right)\subseteq\{v\in I_{2}(n)\mid v\leq w\}. $$

Moreover, $\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{w}(w)=w_{0}\bigl(\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}w}(w_{0}w)\bigr)\neq 0$ , so this spline is genuinely flow-down from $w$ .

For $\alpha\in H$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\alpha\in\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w_{0}w) \displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\ell(w_{0}ws_{\alpha})<\ell(w_{0}w) \displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow n-\ell(ws_{\alpha})<n-\ell(w) \displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\alpha\notin\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w). $$

Therefore $\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w_{0}w)=H\setminus\mathrm{inv}_{H}(w)$ , and $\deg\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{w}=\left\lvert H\right\rvert-\ell_{H}(w)$ .

The dot action is semilinear for the left $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -module structure: $w_{0}\cdot(f\overline{\rho})=w_{0}(f)(w_{0}\cdot\overline{\rho})$ . Since $f\mapsto w_{0}(f)$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ , the splines $\{\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{w}\mid w\in I_{2}(n)\}$ form another homogeneous left $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ -basis of $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . The action of $w_{0}$ also preserves $\left\langle x,y\right\rangle$ , so reducing either basis modulo $\left\langle x,y\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{H}$ gives a homogeneous basis of $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ .

The class $[\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}]$ is one of these quotient basis elements and is therefore nonzero. Corollary 4.7 gives $\dim(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}=1$ , so this class spans the top degree. For each simple reflection $s_{i}$ , conjugation by $w_{0}$ gives $w_{0}s_{i}w_{0}=s_{j}$ for some $j\in\{1,2\}$ , and hence $s_{i}w_{0}=w_{0}s_{j}$ . Since $\alpha_{j}\in H$ , the vertices $w_{0}$ and $s_{i}w_{0}$ are joined by an edge of $\mathcal{G}_{H}$ . The support of $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ is the singleton $\{w_{0}\}$ , so Lemma 4.1 gives $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}-s_{i}\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}=t_{\alpha_{i}}\overline{\tau}_{i}$ for some $\overline{\tau}_{i}\in\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . The right-hand side vanishes in the left quotient. Thus both simple reflections fix $[\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}]$ , and $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\cong\mathbbold{1}$ .

Let $\lambda\colon(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\to\mathbb{C}$ be the invariant linear map satisfying $\lambda([\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}])=1$ . The submodule $\left\langle x,y\right\rangle\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is a homogeneous $I_{2}(n)$ -stable ideal of the spline algebra. Thus $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ is a graded algebra, and the dot action descends to an action by algebra automorphisms. Multiplication and $\lambda$ define a pairing

$$ \langle-,-\rangle_{d}\colon(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d}\otimes(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C},\qquad\langle a,b\rangle_{d}\coloneqq\lambda(ab). $$

For $g\in I_{2}(n)$ , the algebra-automorphism property and the invariance of $\lambda$ give $\langle g\cdot a,g\cdot b\rangle_{d}=\lambda(g\cdot(ab))=\lambda(ab)=\langle a,b\rangle_{d}$ . Hence the pairing is $I_{2}(n)$ -invariant.

Fix $d$ , and list the elements $u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}$ satisfying $\ell_{H}(u_{i})=d$ in a linear extension of Bruhat order, so that $u_{i}\leq u_{j}$ implies $i\leq j$ . The classes $[\overline{\rho}_{u_{1}}],\ldots,[\overline{\rho}_{u_{r}}]$ form a basis of $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d}$ , while $[\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{1}}],\ldots,[\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{r}}]$ form a basis of $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}$ .

Set $M_{ij}\coloneqq\langle[\overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}],[\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{j}}]\rangle_{d}$ . The product $\overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{j}}$ is supported in $\{v\in I_{2}(n)\mid u_{i}\leq v\leq u_{j}\}$ . If $i>j$ , then $u_{i}\nleq u_{j}$ by the choice of linear extension, so this interval is empty and $M_{ij}=0$ . Thus $M$ is upper triangular.

If $\alpha\in\mathrm{inv}_{H}(u_{i})$ , then $u_{i}s_{\alpha}<u_{i}$ , so $\overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}(u_{i}s_{\alpha})=0$ . The spline condition along this edge gives $t_{u_{i}(\alpha)}\mid\overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}(u_{i})$ . If $\alpha\in H\setminus\mathrm{inv}_{H}(u_{i})$ , then $u_{i}s_{\alpha}>u_{i}$ , so $\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{i}}(u_{i}s_{\alpha})=0$ and $t_{u_{i}(\alpha)}\mid\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{i}}(u_{i})$ .

Since $u_{i}$ permutes the roots and $H\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ contains at most one root from each root line, the linear forms $t_{u_{i}(\alpha)}$ , for $\alpha\in H$ , are pairwise nonassociate. The ring $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is a unique factorization domain, so the corresponding products divide the two spline values. Their degrees equal the degrees of the respective splines, and both splines are nonzero at $u_{i}$ . There are therefore $a_{i},b_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ such that

$$ \overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}(u_{i})=a_{i}\prod_{\alpha\in\mathrm{inv}_{H}(u_{i})}t_{u_{i}(\alpha)},\qquad\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{i}}(u_{i})=b_{i}\prod_{\alpha\in H\setminus\mathrm{inv}_{H}(u_{i})}t_{u_{i}(\alpha)}. $$

Any vertex in the supports of both $\overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}$ and $\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{i}}$ must satisfy $u_{i}\leq v\leq u_{i}$ , and hence must equal $u_{i}$ . Their product is therefore supported only at $u_{i}$ , where its value is $a_{i}b_{i}\prod_{\alpha\in H}t_{u_{i}(\alpha)}$ .

The translated top spline $(u_{i}w_{0})\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ has support $(u_{i}w_{0})\{w_{0}\}=\{u_{i}\}$ . Its value at $u_{i}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\bigl((u_{i}w_{0})\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}\bigr)(u_{i}) \displaystyle=u_{i}w_{0}\left(\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}\bigl((u_{i}w_{0})^{-1}u_{i}\bigr)\right) \displaystyle=u_{i}w_{0}\left(\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}(w_{0})\right) \displaystyle=u_{i}w_{0}\left(\prod_{\alpha\in H}t_{w_{0}(\alpha)}\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{\alpha\in H}t_{u_{i}(\alpha)}. $$

The two point-supported splines consequently satisfy

$$ \overline{\rho}_{u_{i}}\overline{\rho}^{\downarrow}_{u_{i}}=a_{i}b_{i}\,(u_{i}w_{0})\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}. $$

Since the top quotient representation is trivial, $[(u_{i}w_{0})\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}]=[\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}]$ , and hence $M_{ii}=a_{i}b_{i}\neq 0$ .

The matrix $M$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, so the pairing is perfect. It induces an $I_{2}(n)$ -equivariant isomorphism $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}\cong(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{d}^{*}$ . Every irreducible representation of $I_{2}(n)$ is self-dual, since every element of $I_{2}(n)$ is conjugate to its inverse. This proves (19). ∎

The following Lemma shows how many copies of the trivial representation appear.

#### Lemma 6.10.

The representation $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ contains a sub-representation isomorphic to

$$ (1+q)(1+q+\cdots+q^{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-1})\,\mathbbold{1}. $$

#### Proof.

Consider different graded pieces of the injection $\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . For $0\leq k\leq h-1$ , the coefficient of $q^{k}$ in $\Hilb(\mathcal{M}_{H};q)$ is the same as in $\Hilb(\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}};q)$ . So this injection must be a surjection, and so $\left(\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}\right)_{k}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{H}\right)_{k}$ for all $0\leq k\leq h-1$ . Since every element of $J$ is degree at least one, $\left(J\mathcal{M}_{\Phi^{+}}\right)_{k}=\left(J\mathcal{M}_{H}\right)_{k}$ for all $1\leq k\leq h$ . Thus, when passing to the quotient, there is an injection

$$ \left(\mathrm{L}_{\Phi^{+}}\right)_{k}\hookrightarrow\left(\mathrm{L}_{H}\right)_{k}\qquad\text{for all}\;\;0\leq k\leq h. $$

So $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ contains a sub-representation isomorphic to $\left(1+2q+\cdots+2q^{h}\right)\mathbbold{1}$ . Proposition 6.9 ensures that $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ also contains $\left(q^{|H|}+2q^{|H|-1}+\cdots+2q^{|H|-h}\right)\mathbbold{1}$ as a sub-representation, and the claim follows. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 6.4.

Set $h=\lfloor|H|/2\rfloor$ . We first construct permutation subrepresentations of $(\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h}$ , then compare their multiplicities with those of $(J\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h}$ to determine $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}$ .

To construct these subrepresentations, we choose degree- $h$ basis splines whose supports allow us to determine their stabilizers and prove independence of their dot-action orbits. Let $z$ be an alternating word of length $t$ ending in $s_{i}$ , where $i\in\{1,2\}$ and $2t\leq n$ . Taking the reflections associated to successive suffixes of the reduced word for $z$ gives

$$ N_{R}(z)=\{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i+2},\ldots,\alpha_{i+2t-2}\}. $$

Since $w_{0}$ interchanges positive and negative roots,

$$ N_{R}(w_{0}z)=\Phi^{+}\setminus N_{R}(z). $$

Suppose first that $|H|=2h$ . Take the two elements $z$ of length $h$ . Their right inversion sets are both contained in $H=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2h}\}$ . The corresponding elements $w_{0}z$ have length $n-h$ and $H$ -length $h$ . Denote them by $w$ and $v$ , with $s_{\alpha}$ the simple left ascent of $w$ and $s_{\beta}$ the simple left ascent of $v$ .

If $|H|=2h+1$ , then $H$ contains exactly one of $\alpha_{2h+1}$ and $\alpha_{2h+2}$ , together with $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2h}$ . Take the unique element $z$ of length $h+1$ whose right inversion set is contained in $H$ , and set $w=w_{0}z$ . Then

$$ \ell(w)=n-h-1,\qquad\ell_{H}(w)=|H|-|N_{R}(z)|=h. $$

Write $s_{\alpha}$ for the simple left ascent of $w$ , and let $\beta$ be the other simple root. We check below that $\alpha$ is $H$ -dominant.

In either case, write $w=w_{0}z$ and $t=\ell(z)$ . The reflection $w^{-1}s_{\alpha}w$ is the reflection of length $2t-1$ corresponding to the last root in the displayed description of $N_{R}(z)$ . In particular, it corresponds to a root in $H$ , so $(w,s_{\alpha}w)\in\mathcal{E}_{H}$ .

On the other hand, if $2t<n$ , then Lemma 4.2, applied to the corresponding simple left ascent of $z$ , gives

$$ \ell(w^{-1}s_{\beta}w)=2t+1. $$

This is larger than the length of every reflection corresponding to a root in $H$ . If $2t=n$ , which can occur here only in the odd case, then $w^{-1}s_{\beta}w$ is the other reflection of length $2t-1=2h+1$ , whose root is not in $H$ . Thus $(w,s_{\beta}w)\notin\mathcal{E}_{H}$ in every case. This verifies the conditions in Definition 6.2. In the even case, the same argument applies to $v$ , with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ interchanged.

Since $H$ is proper, the lengths of these vertices satisfy $2\ell(w)+1>n$ and, in the even case, $2\ell(v)+1>n$ . Thus Theorem 4.5 gives

$$ \overline{\rho}_{w}=\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w}, $$

and similarly $\overline{\rho}_{v}=\partial_{\beta}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\beta}v}$ in the even case. These splines have degree $h$ .

Let

$$ U_{w}=\{u\in I_{2}(n)\mid w\leq u\}. $$

The underlying undirected graph of $\mathcal{G}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ is a cycle of length $2n$ . By the rank-two description of Bruhat order, $U_{w}$ consists of $2t$ consecutive vertices in this cycle, with endpoints $w$ and $s_{\alpha}w$ . The endpoint reflection $w^{-1}s_{\alpha}w$ corresponds to a root in $H$ , so Lemma 5.1 applies. Its proof shows that every vertex of even length in $U_{w}$ is adjacent to every vertex of odd length, with $t$ vertices of each parity. Thus each vertex has $t$ neighbors within $U_{w}$ , and hence $|H|-t=h$ neighbors outside $U_{w}$ .

The spline $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is nonzero and supported within $U_{w}$ , and has degree $h$ . Therefore Corollary 5.2 shows that its support is exactly $U_{w}$ and gives the product formula for its nonzero values. The same conclusions hold for $\overline{\rho}_{v}$ in the even case.

Any element stabilizing $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ must stabilize $U_{w}$ . Since the subgraph induced by $U_{w}$ in the cycle $\mathcal{G}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ is a path, any such element permutes its two endpoints. Left multiplication acts freely on vertices, so the stabilizer of $U_{w}$ has order at most two. Moreover,

$$ s_{\alpha}\cdot\bigl(\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w}\bigr)=\partial_{\alpha}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w}, $$

so $s_{\alpha}$ stabilizes $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ . Hence

$$ \operatorname{Stab}(\overline{\rho}_{w})=\operatorname{Stab}(U_{w})=\left\langle s_{\alpha}\right\rangle. $$

In the even case, the corresponding stabilizers for $\overline{\rho}_{v}$ and $U_{v}$ are $\left\langle s_{\beta}\right\rangle$ .

Left translates of these splines satisfy the product formula in Corollary 5.2 on their translated supports. Since $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ and its support have the same stabilizer, distinct splines in its orbit have distinct supports. The analogous statement holds for $\overline{\rho}_{v}$ . In the even case, the elements $w$ and $v$ have the same length and different simple right ascents. Starting from $w$ or $v$ , the path through its upper order ideal begins with an edge given by right multiplication by its simple right ascent. Each path has $2h-1$ edges, given alternately by right multiplication by the two simple reflections. Thus its first and last edges are given by the same simple reflection, and this reflection differs between the two paths. Left multiplication sends an edge $\{u,us_{i}\}$ to $\{gu,(gu)s_{i}\}$ , so it preserves the simple reflection defining the edge. Therefore no left translate of $U_{w}$ equals $U_{v}$ , and their orbits under left multiplication are disjoint.

Proposition 5.4, with $k=h-1$ , now shows that the dot-action orbits of $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ and $\overline{\rho}_{v}$ in the even case are jointly linearly independent. In the odd case, Corollary 5.5, with $k=h$ , shows that the dot-action orbit of $\overline{\rho}_{w}$ is linearly independent. Their stabilizers therefore give

$$ C_{\alpha}\cong\spann_{\mathbb{C}}\bigl(I_{2}(n)\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w}\bigr), $$

and, in the even case,

$$ C_{\beta}\cong\spann_{\mathbb{C}}\bigl(I_{2}(n)\cdot\overline{\rho}_{v}\bigr). $$

In particular, we have inclusions

$$ \begin{cases}C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}\hookrightarrow(\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h},&|H|=2h,\\
C_{\alpha}\hookrightarrow(\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h},&|H|=2h+1.\end{cases} $$

For $1\leq k<h$ , Lemma 6.10 and Corollary 4.7 give $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{k}\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}$ , while $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{0}\cong\mathbbold{1}$ . Thus equivariant freeness gives, in the representation ring of $I_{2}(n)$ ,

$$ [(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}]=[(\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h}]-[\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{h}]-2\sum_{d=1}^{h-1}[\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{d}]. $$

For $1\leq d<n/2$ , the symmetric powers of the defining representation decompose as

$$ \mathbb{C}[x,y]_{d}\cong\bigoplus_{j=0}^{\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor}V_{d-2j}\oplus\begin{cases}0,&d\text{ is odd},\\
\mathbbold{1},&d\text{ is even}.\end{cases} $$

Since $H$ is proper, $h<n/2$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{h}\oplus 2\bigoplus_{d=1}^{h-1}\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{d} \displaystyle\cong\left(\bigoplus_{d=1}^{h}\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{d}\right)\oplus\left(\bigoplus_{d=1}^{h-1}\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{d}\right) \displaystyle\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus(h-1)}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{h}V_{j}^{\oplus(h+1-j)}. $$

This is the decomposition of the subrepresentation $(J\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h}$ removed in passing to the quotient. In particular, it contains no $V_{j}$ with $j>h$ , no copy of either $\eta_{0}$ or $\eta_{1}$ when $n$ is even, and only one copy of $V_{h}$ .

Since $(J\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h}$ contains no $V_{j}$ with $j>h$ and no $\eta_{i}$ , all copies of these constituents in the permutation subrepresentations constructed above survive in the quotient. In the even case, $C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}$ also supplies two copies of $V_{h}$ , whereas $(J\mathcal{M}_{H})_{h}$ contains only one, so at least one survives. Thus (3) and (16) show that the constituents of

$$ \begin{cases}C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1},&|H|\text{ even},\\
C_{\alpha}-\mathsf{P}_{h},&|H|\text{ odd},\end{cases} $$

survive in $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}$ with at least the indicated multiplicities.

Lemma 6.10 gives two trivial constituents in degree $h$ , and Corollary 4.7 leaves no room for any other irreducible summands. Thus, when $|H|$ is even,

$$ (\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}\oplus\left(C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1}\right). $$

When $|H|$ is odd,

$$ (\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}\oplus\left(C_{\alpha}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right), $$

and Proposition 6.9 gives the same decomposition in degree $h+1$ .

Finally, Proposition 6.9 determines the remaining upper degrees from the lower degrees already computed. In particular, $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{k}\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}$ for $|H|-h<k<|H|$ , and $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{|H|}\cong\mathbbold{1}$ . This proves the stated formula. ∎

#### Corollary 6.11.

The left representation $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ is not always a permutation representation. Moreover, this can fail in the first degree.

#### Proof.

For $n=5$ and $H=\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}\}$ , Theorem 6.4 gives, after forgetting the grading,

$$ \mathrm{L}_{H}\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 6}\oplus V_{2}^{\oplus 2}. $$

Its character value at $r$ is $6+4\cos(4\pi/5)=5-\sqrt{5}$ . Since permutation characters take nonnegative integer values, $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ is not a permutation representation. For the same representation we also get that $(\mathrm{L}_{H})_{1}\cong\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus 2}\oplus V_{2}$ , whose character value at $r$ is $2+2\cos(4\pi/5)=\frac{1}{2}(3-\sqrt{5})$ , which is also irrational. ∎

## 7. The Right Representation

This section will compute the right action representation $\mathrm{R}_{H}$ in Theorem 7.3. The proof will leverage equivariant freeness and Theorem 6.4, and follow a similar structure as the previous section.

Since $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ is free over the right action as well as the left, there is a noncanonical isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{M}_{H}\cong\mathbb{C}[\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathrm{R}_{H}\cong\left(\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus i+1}q^{i}\right)\otimes\mathrm{R}_{H} $$

of graded $I_{2}(n)$ -representations, where $I_{2}(n)$ acts diagonally on the right-hand side. Consequently,

$$ \left(\mathcal{M}_{H}\right)_{d}\cong\bigoplus_{j=0}^{d}\mathbbold{1}^{\oplus j+1}\otimes(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{d-j}\cong\bigoplus_{j=0}^{d}(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{d-j}^{\oplus j+1}. $$

#### Proposition 7.1.

The top graded piece of $\mathrm{R}_{H}$ is the sign representation. For every $0\leq d\leq\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ , multiplication in the graded algebra $\mathrm{R}_{H}$ restricts to a perfect $I_{2}(n)$ -equivariant pairing

$$ (\mathrm{R}_{H})_{d}\otimes(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}\longrightarrow(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\cong\sgn. $$

Consequently,

$$ \sgn\otimes(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert-d}\cong(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{d} $$

as $I_{2}(n)$ -representations.

#### Proof.

We will compute $(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{|H|}$ directly. The rest of the statement follows exactly as it does in the proof of Proposition 6.9 with the $\sgn$ -tensor instead of the trivial tensor.

Let $\alpha$ be a simple root and $\overline{r}_{\gamma}$ be the spline in $\mathbb{C}[\overline{x}_{r},\overline{y}_{r}]$ whose evaluation at $w$ is $t_{w(\gamma)}$ . The following table gives evaluations of splines at $w_{0}$ and $s_{\alpha}w_{0}$ for several splines in $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ . Each follows directly from their definitions.

|  | $s_{\alpha}w_{0}$ | $w_{0}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ | $0$ | $\displaystyle\prod_{\gamma\in H}t_{w_{0}(\gamma)}$ |
| $s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ | $\displaystyle\prod_{\gamma\in H}s_{\alpha}t_{w_{0}(\gamma)}$ | $0$ |
| $\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w_{0}}$ | $\displaystyle\frac{-1}{t_{\alpha}}\prod_{\gamma\in H}t_{s_{\alpha}w_{0}(\gamma)}$ | $\displaystyle\frac{1}{t_{\alpha}}\prod_{\gamma\in H}t_{w_{0}(\gamma)}$ |
| $\overline{r}_{w_{0}(\alpha)}$ | $-t_{\alpha}$ | $t_{\alpha}$ |

So $s_{\alpha}\cdot\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}=\overline{r}_{w_{0}(\alpha)}\overline{\rho}_{s_{\alpha}w_{0}}-\overline{\rho}_{w_{0}}$ . Since the same holds replacing $\alpha$ with the other simple root $\beta$ and $(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}$ is one-dimensional, we get $(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{\left\lvert H\right\rvert}\cong\sgn$ . ∎

#### Lemma 7.2.

Let $H\neq\Phi^{+}$ . The representation $\mathrm{R}_{H}$ contains a sub-representation isomorphic to

$$ \mathsf{Co}_{H}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\mathbbold{1}+V_{1}\,q+\cdots+V_{h}\,q^{h}+V_{h-1}\,q^{h+1}+\cdots+V_{1}\,q^{2h-1}+\sgn q^{2h}&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h\\
\mathbbold{1}+V_{1}\,q+\cdots+V_{h}\,q^{h}+V_{h}\,q^{h+1}+\cdots+V_{1}\,q^{2h}+\sgn q^{2h+1}&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h+1.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

The proof that

$$ \mathbbold{1}+V_{1}q+\cdots+V_{h}q^{h} $$

appears as a sub-representation is exactly the same as that of Lemma 6.10, replacing $\mathrm{L}_{H}$ with $\mathrm{R}_{H}$ . Note that since $H\neq\Phi^{+}$ , we never see the middle degree of the coinvariant algebra appear when $n$ is even.

The remaining graded sub-representations appear as a consequence of Proposition 7.1, since $\sgn\otimes V_{i}\cong V_{i}$ and $\sgn\otimes\mathbbold{1}\cong\sgn$ . ∎

#### Theorem 7.3.

Let $H\subsetneq\Phi^{+}$ be a Hessenberg space, let $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ be the simple roots, and set $h=\lfloor|H|/2\rfloor$ . If $\left\lvert H\right\rvert$ is odd, let $\alpha$ be the $H$ -dominant simple root. Recall the definition of $\mathsf{Co}_{H}$ in Lemma 7.2 as well as $\mathsf{P}_{h}$ in Section 6. Then, as an element of the graded representation ring of $I_{2}(n)$ ,

$$ \mathrm{R}_{H}\cong\begin{cases}\displaystyle\mathsf{Co}_{H}\oplus q^{h}\left(C_{\alpha}\oplus C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}-\mathsf{P}_{h-1}\right),&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h,\\[10.0pt]
\displaystyle\mathsf{Co}_{H}\oplus q^{h}\left(C_{\alpha}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right)\oplus q^{h+1}\left(C_{\beta}-\mathsf{P}_{h}\right),&\text{if }\left\lvert H\right\rvert=2h+1.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

Comparing equations (18) and (21) with Lemmas 6.10 and 7.2 at degree $h$ , one gets

$$ (\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}\oplus(h-1)\,\mathbbold{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{h}(h+1-j)V_{j}\cong(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{h}\oplus(h+1)\,\mathbbold{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{h-1}(h+1-j)V_{j}. $$

Canceling, we get

$$ (\mathrm{L}_{H})_{h}\oplus V_{h}\cong(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{h}\oplus 2\mathbbold{1}. $$

Comparing with Theorem 6.4 $(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{h}$ computes as claimed. If $(\mathrm{R}_{H})_{h+1}$ is needed, then Proposition 7.1 applies, noting that when $n$ is even then $\eta_{\alpha}\otimes\sgn=\eta_{\beta}$ . The remaining graded pieces are handled by Lemma 7.2 for dimension reasons. ∎

# A tiling property for actions of amenable groups along Tempelman Følner sequencesThanks: The first author conducted research through the summer research USRA program at McGill University under the supervision of Marcin Sabok supported by NSERC Discovery Grant RGPIN 2015-03738.

**Authors:** Jonathan Boretsky and Jenna Zomback

## Abstract

We show that a certain tiling property (which directly implies the pointwise ergodic theorem) holds for pmp actions of amenable groups along increasing Tempelman Følner sequences, thus providing a short and combinatorial proof of the corresponding pointwise ergodic theorem.

## 1. Introduction

For a group $\Gamma$ acting on a probability space $X$ and a sequence $(F_{n})$ of finite subsets of $\Gamma$ , the pointwise ergodic property for $\Gamma$ along $(F_{n})$ says that the action of $\Gamma$ is ergodic if and only if for every $L^{1}$ function $f$ on $X$ , the integral (the global average) of $f$ over $X$ is equal to the limit of the averages of $f$ over $F_{n}\cdot x$ (the pointwise average) for almost every $x\in X$ . The classical ergodic theorem, due to G. D. Birkhoff in 1931 [1], says that probability measure preserving (pmp) actions of $\mathbb{Z}$ along the sequence $[0,n)$ have the pointwise ergodic property. In 2001, E. Lindenstrauss proved that actions of amenable groups along tempered Følner sequences have the pointwise ergodic property [5].

A. Tserunyan in [8] gives a short, combinatorial proof of the classical pointwise ergodic theorem (for $\mathbb{Z}$ ) by reducing it to showing that the following tiling property holds for pmp actions of $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}$ along the intervals $F_{n}=[0,n)$ :

#### Definition 1 (Tiling Property).

We say that a pmp action of a countable group $\Gamma$ on a standard probability space $(X,\mu)$ has the tiling property along a sequence $(F_{n})$ of finite subsets of $\Gamma$ if for any pointwise increasing sequence of measurable functions $\ell_{n}:X\to\mathbb{N}$ , $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , and $\epsilon>0$ , there are arbitrarily large finite subsets $T\subseteq\Gamma$ such that for a set of points $x$ of measure at least $(1-\epsilon)$ , $T\cdot x$ can be covered up to $\epsilon$ fraction by disjoint sets of the form $F_{\ell_{i}(y)}\cdot y$ (where $T\cdot x$ and $F_{\ell_{i}(y)}\cdot y$ are treated as multisets if the action of $\Gamma$ is not free).

It is also implicit in [8] that the tiling property implies the pointwise ergodic theorem for any pmp group action (see Section 3 for a proof). This implication distills out the analytic part from the proofs of pointwise ergodic theorems, reducing them to combinatorial (finitary) tiling problems. Another proof of the ergodic theorem for $\mathbb{Z}$ revolving around the same idea was given in [4].

In this paper, we prove that the tiling property holds for pmp actions of amenable groups along increasing Tempelman Følner sequences $(F_{n})$ by finding Vitali covers with Følner tiles on multiple scales. As a consequence, we prove the corresponding pointwise ergodic theorem:

#### Theorem 2 (Pointwise ergodic).

Fix a pmp action of an amenable group $\Gamma$ on a standard probability space $(X,\mu)$ and an increasing Tempelman Følner sequence $(F_{n})$ . Then the action of $\Gamma$ on $X$ is ergodic if and only if for every $f\in L^{1}(X,\mu)$ ,

$$ \lim_{n}A_{f}[F_{n}\cdot x]=\int_{X}f(x)d\mu(x)\text{ a.e.} $$

where $A_{f}[F_{n}\cdot x]\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\frac{1}{|F_{n}|}\sum_{\gamma\in F_{n}}f(\gamma\cdot x)$ .

Although this is less general than Lindenstrauss’s theorem, our proof is shorter and offers the advantage that the methods used are more elementary and finitary.

Many people have shown this result for increasing Tempelman Følner sequences. The shortest proof of Theorem 2 that the authors are aware of is given in [6], which uses a Vitali covering lemma along with basic functional analysis: a function $f\in L^{1}(X,\mu)$ is approximated by functions for which the ergodic theorem holds trivially, and the error is controlled by applying the Vitali covering lemma. Other proofs include [2] and [7], which also use a Vitali covering lemma along with analysis. However, none of these proofs yield the tiling property described above, and hence they do not take advantage of the abstract implication of the corresponding pointwise ergodic theorem.

### A word on the proof of the tiling property

Compared to [8], the tiling property is much harder to establish for general increasing Tempelman Følner sequences. For example, tiling $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ with boxes of different given sizes for each center is harder than tiling $\mathbb{Z}$ with intervals. The key idea in mitigating this difficulty is to iterate the Vitali covering lemma to find covers on multiple scales. We essentially zoom very far out, cover some constant fraction of the space with large sets (this fraction comes from the Tempelman condition and is independent of how far we’ve zoomed out), and then zoom in on the spots we miss, and fill those in as best we can with smaller sets, and so on and so forth. Since we cover a constant fraction on each scale, if we zoom out far enough at the beginning, once we zoom all the way back in, we will have covered nearly the whole space.

### Organization

In Section 2, we provide the necessary definitions and notation that will be used throughout the paper. In Section 3, we give an explicit proof, due to Tserunyan, that Definition 1 implies the pointwise ergodic property for any pmp group action. In Section 4, we establish the tiling property for pmp actions of amenable groups along increasing Tempelman Følner sequences, which then directly implies the corresponding pointwise ergodic property.

#### Acknowledgements.

The authors would like to thank their advisors, Marcin Sabok and Anush Tserunyan, for their guidance, suggestions, and support. Many thanks as well to Benjamin Weiss for pointing out the proof of Theorem 2 given in [6], and to Alexander Kechris for useful suggestions.

## 2. Definitions and notation

Let $(X,\mu)$ be a standard probability space, and a function $f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ . For a finite set $A\subseteq X$ , define the average of $f$ over $A$ , $A_{f}[A]\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{x\in A}f(x)$ . For a finite equivalence relation $F$ on $X$ , define $A_{f}[F](x)\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=A_{f}[[x]_{F}]$ . Given a group $\Gamma$ and a finite set $R$ , define the $R$ -boundary of a set $S$ , denoted $\partial_{R}S$ , to be the set of points $s$ for which $Rs\cap S\neq\emptyset$ and $R_{s}\cap S^{c}\neq\emptyset$ .

A sequence $(F_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of finite subsets of $\Gamma$ is a Følner sequence if $\Gamma=\bigcup_{n}F_{n}$ and $\lim_{n}\frac{|\partial_{R}F_{n}|}{|F_{n}|}=0$ for all finite sets $R$ . A group $\Gamma$ is called amenable if it admits a Følner sequence. For this paper, we will assume that our Følner sequences are increasing.

Given a Følner sequence $(F_{n})$ , we say $(F_{n})$ is tempered if there is some natural number $C$ such that for all $n$ ,

$$ \left|\bigcup_{k<n}F_{k}^{-1}F_{n}\right|\leq C|F_{n}| $$

and Tempelman if there is $C$ such that for all $n$ ,

$$ \left|\bigcup_{k\leq n}F_{k}^{-1}F_{n}\right|\leq C|F_{n}| $$

in the latter case, we’ll call the smallest such $C$ the Tempelman constant of $(F_{n})$ . Note that any Tempelman Følner sequence is tempered.

Every amenable group has a tempered Følner sequence (in fact, every Følner sequence has a tempered subsequence). In [5]*Example 4.2, an example is given of an amenable group without a Tempelman Følner sequence. However, [3]*Theorem 3.4 gives a sufficient condition for the existence of a Tempelman Følner sequence:

#### Theorem 3 (Hochman 2007).

If for a countable, abelian, amenable group $G$ , we have

$$ r(G)=\sup\{n\in\mathbb{N}:G\text{ contains a subgroup isomorphic to }\mathbb{Z}^{n}\}<\infty $$

then $G$ possesses at least one Tempelman Følner sequence.

## 3. The tiling property implies the pointwise ergodic theorem

The following result is implicitly stated in [8] and was explained by Tserunyan to the second author.

#### Theorem 4 (Tserunyan).

Assume $\Gamma$ has the tiling property along a sequence of finite subsets $(F_{n})$ . Then for any pmp action of $\Gamma$ on a standard probability space $(X,\mu)$ , the action of $\Gamma$ on $X$ is ergodic if and only if for every $f\in L^{1}(X,\mu)$ ,

$$ \lim_{n}A_{f}[F_{n}\cdot x]=\int_{X}f(x)d\mu(x)\text{ a.e.} $$

where $A_{f}[F_{n}\cdot x]\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\frac{1}{|F_{n}|}\sum_{\gamma\in F_{n}}f(\gamma\cdot x)$ .

#### Proof.

By replacing $f$ with $f-\int f$ , we may assume without loss of generality that $\int f=0$ . We will show that ${f}^{*}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_{f}[F_{n}\cdot x]\leq 0$ a.e., and an analogous argument shows ${f}_{*}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}A_{f}[F_{n}\cdot x]\geq 0$ a.e.

Since ${f}^{*}$ is $T$ -invariant, ergodicity implies that it is some constant $C$ almost everywhere. Assume by way of contradiction that $C>c>0$ . Define $\ell_{i}:X\to\mathbb{N}$ by $x\mapsto$ the $i^{\text{th}}$ $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A_{f}[F_{n}x]>c$ (equivalently, $A_{f-c}[F_{n}x]>0$ ).

Fix $\delta>0$ small enough so that for any measurable $Y\subseteq X$ , $\mu(Y)<\delta$ implies $\int_{Y}(f-c)\,d\mu>-\frac{c}{3}$ , and let $M\in\mathbb{N}$ be large enough so that the set $Y\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=f^{-1}(-M,\infty)$ has measure at least $1-\delta$ .

The tiling property applied to the function $\ell_{i}$ with $\varepsilon\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\frac{1}{2(M+c)}\frac{c}{3}$ gives a finite $T\subseteq\Gamma$ such that $\mu(Z)\geq 1-\varepsilon$ , where $Z$ is the set of all $x\in X$ such that at least $1-\varepsilon$ fraction of $T\cdot x$ is partitioned into sets of the form $\ell_{i}(y)\cdot y$ .

#### Claim.

For each $x\in Z$ , $A_{\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)}[T\cdot x]\geq-(M+c)\varepsilon$ .

#### Proof of Claim 1.

By the definition of $Z$ , on a subset $B\subseteq T\cdot x$ that occupies at least $1-\varepsilon$ fraction of $T\cdot x$ , the average of $f-c$ is positive, and hence that of $\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)\mathord{\downharpoonright_{B}}$ is non-negative. On the remaining set $T\cdot x\setminus B$ , the function $\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)$ is at least $-(M+c)$ , by the definition of $Y$ . Thus, the average of $\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)$ on the entire $T\cdot x$ is at least $-(M+c)\varepsilon$ .

Now we compute using this claim and the invariance of $\mu$ :

$$ \displaystyle\int_{Y}(f-c)\,d\mu \displaystyle=\int_{X}A_{\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)}[T\cdot x]\,d\mu(x) \displaystyle=\int_{Z}A_{\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)}[T\cdot x]\,d\mu(x)+\int_{X\setminus Z}A_{\mathbb{1}_{Y}(f-c)}[T\cdot x]\,d\mu(x) \displaystyle\geq-(M+c)\varepsilon-(M+c)\varepsilon=-2(M+c)\varepsilon=-\frac{c}{3}. $$

This gives a contradiction:

$$ \displaystyle 0=\int_{X}f\,d\mu \displaystyle=c+\int_{X}(f-c)\,d\mu \displaystyle=c+\int_{Y}(f-c)\,d\mu+\int_{X\setminus Y}(f-c)\,d\mu \displaystyle>c-\frac{c}{3}-\frac{c}{3}>0.\qed $$

## 4. The tiling property for increasing Tempelman Følner sequences

In this section, we prove the following:

#### Lemma 5.

The tiling property holds for pmp actions of amenable groups along increasing Tempelman Følner sequences.

As a corollary, by Theorem 4, we obtain Theorem 2. In order to prove this lemma, we need a Vitali covering lemma. For the rest of this section, fix an amenable group $\Gamma$ and Tempelman Følner sequence $F_{i}$ with Tempelman constant $C$ , standard probability space $(X,\mu)$ on which $\Gamma$ acts in a pmp way, and $\epsilon>0$ .

#### Lemma 6 (Vitali covering).

Given a function $l:X\rightarrow N$ and a finite subset $S\subseteq X$ , there exists a set $K$ , which is a disjoint union of sets of the form $F_{l(x)}x$ , $x\in S$ , such that $|K|\geq\frac{1}{C}|S\cup K|$ .

#### Proof.

Put $=S=\{x_{1},...,x_{n}\}$ , $D_{0}=K_{0}=\emptyset$ . We will inductively define increasing sets $K_{i}$ and $D_{i}$ for $i\leq n$ until $S\setminus D_{i}=\emptyset$ . Assume $S\setminus D_{i}\neq\emptyset$ . Let $t=\max_{x\in S\setminus{D_{i}}}l(x)$ , and let $j$ be least such that $x_{j}\in S\setminus D_{i}$ and $l(x_{j})=t$ . Put $K_{i+1}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=K_{i}\cup F_{t}x_{j}$ and $D_{i+1}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=D_{i}\cup F_{t}^{-1}F_{T}\cdot x_{j}$ . Iterate this (up to $n$ times) until $S\setminus D_{m}=\emptyset$ for some $m\leq n$ . Put $K\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=K_{m}$ and $D\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=D_{m}$ .

We claim that the selected $F_{T}\cdot x_{j}$ are actually pairwise disjoint. If not, suppose that at the $(i+1)^{\text{th}}$ step there is some $y\in F_{T}\cdot x_{j}\cap K_{i}$ . Then $x_{j}\in F_{t}^{-1}y$ . But since $y\in K_{i}$ , there is some $t^{\prime}\geq t$ and $j^{\prime}$ such that $y\in F_{t^{\prime}}x_{j^{\prime}}$ . Hence $x_{j}\in F_{t}^{-1}F_{t^{\prime}}x_{j^{\prime}}\subseteq F_{t^{\prime}}^{-1}F_{t^{\prime}}x_{j^{\prime}}\subseteq D_{i}$ , contradicting our choice of $x_{j}$ .

So at each step, we add exactly $|F_{t}|$ elements to $K$ and at most $C|F_{t}|$ elements to $D$ . Hence, $|K|\geq\frac{1}{C}|D|\geq\frac{1}{C}|S\cup K|$ since $S\cup K\subseteq D$ . ∎

Now we may begin proving Lemma 5. The idea is to break our space into large finite sets. We will tile each of these finite sets with Følner shapes of various sizes, using progressively smaller Følner shapes to fill in whatever holes remain after placing the larger Følner shapes.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.

First, fix $r\in\mathbb{N}$ large enough so that $\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{r}<\frac{\epsilon}{2}$ . We will ultimately pick $r$ many “good” sizes of tiles for a large fraction of the points in $X$ . Fix $r$ many functions $G_{i}:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that $G_{1}(x)\geq\frac{2}{C}(x)$ and for $i>1$ , $G_{i}(x)\geq\frac{C-1}{C}G_{i-1}(x)+(i+1)(x)$ where each $G_{i}$ is continuous and $G_{i}(0)=0$ . For example, $G_{i}(x)\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{i}x+\sum_{k=1}^{i+1}kx$ is such a collection of functions. Fix $\alpha$ small enough so that $\beta\leq\alpha\implies G_{r}(\beta)<\frac{\epsilon}{2}$ . Put $\eta\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\min(\alpha,\epsilon)$ .

For each $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $C_{n}^{(p)}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\{x\in X:(\exists i\in\mathbb{N})\;l_{i}(x)\in[p,n]\}$ . Since the $l_{i}$ are strictly increasing in $x$ for all $x$ , $\bigcup_{n}C_{n}^{(p)}=X$ . Hence, there is some large enough $p^{*}$ such that $\mu(C_{p^{*}}^{(p)})>1-\frac{\eta^{2}}{r}$ . This means that for any $r$ -many values $p_{j}$ ( $0\leq j<r$ ),

$$ \mu(\{x\in X:(\forall j<r)\;(\exists i\in\mathbb{N})\;l_{i}(x)\in[p_{j},p_{j}^{*}]\})>1-\eta^{2}. $$

We define two sequences of natural numbers of length $r$ as follows. Let $L_{0}$ be large enough so that $\frac{|\partial_{F_{r}}F_{n}|}{|F_{n}|}<\eta$ for all $n>L_{0}$ . For $i<r$ , define $R_{i}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=L_{i}^{*}$ , and $L_{i+1}>R_{i}$ large enough so that

$$ \frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{i}}}F_{n}|}{|F_{n}|}<\frac{\eta}{|F_{R_{i}}|} $$

for all $n\geq L_{i+1}$ . Put $\delta\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\frac{\eta}{|F_{R_{r-1}}|}$ . We will think of the $[L_{j},R_{j}]$ as ranges of allowable sizes for out tiles. Finally, Let $T\subseteq\Gamma$ satisfy $\frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{r-1}}}T|}{|T|}<\delta$ .

Define parial functions $p_{i}(x)\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=l_{j}(x)$ where $j$ is smallest such that $l_{j}(x)\in[L_{i},R_{i}]$ if such a $j$ exists. Set $P\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\left\{x\in X:\;(\forall i<r)\;x\in\text{dom}(p_{i})\right\}$ . Hence, $\mu(P)>1-\eta^{2}$ , so $\mu(\left\{x\in X:A_{\mathbb{1}_{P}}[T\cdot x]<1-\eta\right\})\leq\eta$ , because otherwise, setting $B\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\left\{x\in X:A_{\mathbb{1}_{P}}[T\cdot x]<1-\eta\right\}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 1-\eta^{2}<\mu(P) \displaystyle=\int_{X}\mathbb{1}_{P}(x)d\mu(x) \displaystyle[\text{by the invariance of }\mu] \displaystyle=\int_{X}\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{\gamma\in T}\mathbb{1}_{P}(\gamma\cdot x)d\mu(x) \displaystyle=\int_{X}A_{\mathbb{1}_{P}}[T\cdot x]\;d\mu(x) \displaystyle=\int_{X\setminus B}A_{\mathbb{1}_{P}}[T\cdot x]\;d\mu(x)+\int_{B}A_{\mathbb{1}_{P}}[T\cdot x]\;d\mu(x) \displaystyle\leq\mu(X\setminus B)+\mu(B)(1-\eta) \displaystyle<1-\eta+\eta(1-\eta)=1-\eta^{2} $$

Hence, at least $1-\eta$ fraction of points $x\in X$ have $1-\eta$ fraction of points of $T\cdot x$ lying in $P$ . Since $\eta\leq\epsilon$ , it now suffices to show that for a point $x$ such that at least $1-\eta$ fraction of $T\cdot x$ is contained in $P$ , we can tile $T\cdot x$ up to $\epsilon$ fraction with tiles of the form $F_{l_{i}(x)}x$ .

We claim that in $k$ steps, $1\leq k\leq r$ , we can tile $T\cdot x$ up to $\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{k}+G_{k}(\eta)$ fraction. As discussed earlier, we will start by tiling with our largest Følner shapes, i.e. $l_{i}(x)\in[L_{r},R_{r}]$ , and in each step we will move down a size.

In step $k$ , apply Lemma 6 with $l=p_{r-k}$ and

$$ S_{k}\mathrel{\vbox{\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}=\{x\in T\cdot x\cap\text{dom}(p_{r-k}):F_{R_{r-k}}x\text{ is contained in the set of uncovered points in }T\} $$

so that the constructed set of tiles $K_{k}$ is contained in the set of uncovered points in $T$ .

See Fig. 1 for a sketch of the tiling process for $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . In the first picture, we place the tiles from $K_{1}$ , and in the second picture we remove strips along the boundaries of $T\cdot x$ as well as $K_{1}$ . We also mark the points $y$ and $z$ for which $p_{r-2}$ is not defined. Applying Lemma 6 to $S_{2}$ (the remaining points), we place smaller tiles, seen in a lighter color in the third picture.

*Figure 1. Identifying the set $S_{2}$ and placing the set of tiles $K_{2}$ when $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{2}$*

Now, $S_{k}$ is almost all of the uncovered points in $T$ except possibly:

- (1) A small strip along the boundary of $T$ , of size $|\partial_{F_{R_{r-k}}}T||F_{R_{r-k}}|<\eta|T|$ since $\frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{r-k}}}T|}{|T|}<\frac{\eta}{|F_{R_{r-}k}|}$ .

- (2) The set of points on which $p_{r-k}$ is not defined, which has fewer than $\eta|T|$ points.

- (3) A small strip along the boundary of the covered points from each of the previous $k-1$ steps. Fix $j<k$ , and consider the set $K_{j}$ of covered points from the $j^{\text{th}}$ step. We might miss a strip of size $|\partial_{F_{R_{r-k}}}K_{j}||F_{R_{r-k}}|$ . Note that since the boundary of $K_{j}$ consists of Følner shapes of sizes in $[L_{r-j},R_{r-j}]$ , we have $\frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{r-k}}}K_{j}|}{|K_{j}|}\leq\frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{r-j}}}F_{R_{r-j}}|}{|F_{R_{r-j}}|}$ , so $\displaystyle|\partial_{F_{R_{r-k}}}K_{j}||F_{R_{r-k}}|$ $\displaystyle\leq\frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{r-j}}}F_{R_{r-j}}|}{|F_{R_{r-j}}|}|K_{j}||F_{R_{r-k}}|$ $\displaystyle\leq\frac{\eta}{|F_{R_{r-j-1}}|}|K_{j}||F_{R_{r-k}}|$ $\displaystyle\leq\eta|T|,$ where the penultimate inequality comes from our choice of $L_{r-j}$ to be large enough that $n\geq L_{r-j}$ implies $\frac{|\partial_{F_{R_{r-j}}}F_{n}|}{|F_{n}|}<\frac{\eta}{|F_{R_{r-j-1}}|}$ , and the final inequality comes from $K_{j}\subseteq T$ and the fact that $r-k\leq r-j-1$ for any $j<k$ .

In total, $S_{k}$ is missing at most $(k+1)\eta|T|$ uncovered points from $T$ . If $k=1$ , we have that $K_{1}$ covers at least $\frac{1}{C}$ fraction of $S_{1}\cup K_{1}$ , and $|S_{1}\cup K_{1}|\geq(1-2\eta)|T|$ . So $K_{1}$ covers at least $\frac{1}{C}(1-2\eta)|T|$ , and we are left with $\frac{C-1+2\eta}{C}|T|$ , so we cover all but $\frac{C-1}{C}+G_{1}(\eta)$ fraction of $|T|$ .

If $k\geq 2$ , assume $\bigcup_{i<k}K_{i}$ covers all but $\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{k-1}+G_{k-1}(\eta)$ fraction of $T$ . Notice that

$$ |S_{k}\cup K_{k}|\leq\left(\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{k-1}+G_{k-1}(\eta)\right)|T|, $$

since both $S_{k}$ and $K_{k}$ are contained in the set of uncovered points of $T$ . Since $K_{k}$ covers at least $\frac{1}{C}$ fraction of $|S_{k}\cup K_{k}|$ , at most $\frac{C-1}{C}$ fraction of $|S_{k}\cup K_{k}|$ is left uncovered. So $\bigcup_{i\leq k}K_{k}$ covers all of $T$ but at most

$$ \displaystyle(k+1)\eta|T|+\frac{C-1}{C}|S_{k}\cup K_{k}| \displaystyle\leq\left((k+1)\eta+\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{k}+\frac{C-1}{C}G_{k-1}(\eta)\right)|T| \displaystyle\leq\left(\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{k}+G_{k}(\eta)\right)|T| $$

many points. This concludes the proof of our claim. Iterate this algorithm $r$ times so that we have covered all but $\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{r}+G_{r}(\eta)$ fraction of $T$ . Since, by hypothesis, both $\left(\frac{C-1}{C}\right)^{r},G_{r}(\eta)<\frac{\epsilon}{2}$ , this concludes the proof. ∎

# Polyhedral and tropical geometry of flag positroids

**Authors:** Jonathan Boretsky, Christopher Eur, Lauren Williams Address: Centre de Recherches Mathématiques in Montreal Email address: jonathan.boretsky@mail.mcgill.ca Address: Carnegie Mellon University Email address: ceur@cmu.edu Address: Harvard University Email address: williams@math.harvard.edu

## Abstract

A flag positroid of ranks $\mathbf{r}:=(r_{1}<\dots<r_{k})$ on $[n]$ is a flag matroid that can be realized by a real $r_{k}\times n$ matrix $A$ such that the $r_{i}\times r_{i}$ minors of $A$ involving rows $1,2,\dots,r_{i}$ are nonnegative for all $1\leq i\leq k$ . In this paper we explore the polyhedral and tropical geometry of flag positroids, particularly when $\mathbf{r}:=(a,a+1,\dots,b)$ is a sequence of consecutive numbers. In this case we show that the nonnegative tropical flag variety $\TrFl_{\mathbf{r},n}^{\geq 0}$ equals the nonnegative flag Dressian $\FlDr_{\mathbf{r},n}^{\geq 0}$ , and that the points ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}=(\mu_{a},\ldots,\mu_{b})$ of $\TrFl_{\mathbf{r},n}^{\geq 0}=\FlDr_{\mathbf{r},n}^{\geq 0}$ give rise to coherent subdivisions of the flag positroid polytope $P(\underline{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}})$ into flag positroid polytopes. Our results have applications to Bruhat interval polytopes: for example, we show that a complete flag matroid polytope is a Bruhat interval polytope if and only if its $(\leq 2)$ -dimensional faces are Bruhat interval polytopes. Our results also have applications to realizability questions. We define a positively oriented flag matroid to be a sequence of positively oriented matroids $(\chi_{1},\dots,\chi_{k})$ which is also an oriented flag matroid. We then prove that every positively oriented flag matroid of ranks $\mathbf{r}=(a,a+1,\dots,b)$ is realizable.

#### Contents

- 2 Background on total positivity and Bruhat interval polytopes

- 3 The nonnegative tropicalization

- 4 Positively oriented flag matroids

- 5 Subdivisions of flag matroid polytopes

- 6 Three-term incidence relations

- 7 Projections of positive Richardsons to positroids

- 8 Fan structures for and coherent subdivisions from $\TrGr_{d;n}^{>0}$ and $\TrFl_{n}^{>0}$

- References

## 1. Introduction

In recent years there has been a great deal of interest in the tropical Grassmannian [SS04, HJJS08, HJS14, CEGM19, Bos21], and matroid polytopes and their subdivisions [Spe08, AFR10, Ear22], as well as “positive” [Pos, SW05, Oh08, ARW16, LF19, LPW20, SW21, AHLS20] and “flag” [TW15, BEZ21, BLMM17, JL22, JLLO, Bor22] versions of the above objects. The aim of this paper is to illustrate the beautiful relationships between the nonnegative tropical flag variety, the nonnegative flag Dressian, and flag positroid polytopes and their subdivisions, unifying and generalizing some of the existing results. We will particularly focus on the case of flag varieties (respectively, flag positroids) consisting of subspaces (respectively, matroids) of consecutive ranks. This case includes both Grassmannians and complete flag varieties.

For positive integers $n$ and $d$ with $d<n$ , we let $[n]$ denote the set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and we let ${[n]\choose d}$ denote the collection of all $d$ -element subsets of $[n]$ . Given a subset $S\subseteq[n]$ we let $\mathbf{e}_{S}$ denote the sum of standard basis vectors $\sum_{i\in S}\mathbf{e}_{i}$ . For a collection $\mathcal{B}\subset{[n]\choose d}$ , we let

$$ P(\mathcal{B})=\text{the convex hull of $\{\mathbf{e}_{B}:B\in\mathcal{B}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$}. $$

The collection $\mathcal{B}$ is said to define a matroid $M$ of rank $d$ on $[n]$ if every edge of the polytope $P(\mathcal{B})$ is parallel to $\mathbf{e}_{i}-\mathbf{e}_{j}$ for some $i\neq j\in[n]$ . In this case, we call $\mathcal{B}$ the set of bases of $M$ , and define the matroid polytope $P(M)$ of $M$ to be the polytope $P(\mathcal{B})$ . When $\mathcal{B}$ indexes the nonvanishing Plücker coordinates of an element $A$ of the Grassmannian $\Gr_{d,n}(\mathbb{C})$ , we say that $A$ realizes $M$ , and it is well-known that $P(\mathcal{B})$ is the moment map image of the closure of the torus orbit of $A$ in the Grassmannian [GGMS87]. We assume familiarity with the fundamentals of matroid theory as in [Oxl11] and [BGW03].

The above definition of matroid in terms of its polytope is due to [GGMS87]. Flag matroids are natural generalizations of matroids that admit the following polytopal definition.

#### Definition 1.1.

[BGW03, Corollary 1.13.5 and Theorem 1.13.6] Let $\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{k})$ be a sequence of increasing integers in $[n]$ . A flag matroid of ranks $\mathbf{r}$ on $[n]$ is a sequence ${\boldsymbol{M}}=(M_{1},\ldots,M_{k})$ of matroids of ranks $(r_{1},\ldots,r_{k})$ on $[n]$ such that all vertices of the polytope

$$ P({\boldsymbol{M}})=P(M_{1})+\cdots+P(M_{k}),\text{ the Minkowski sum of matroid polytopes}, $$

are equidistant from the origin. The polytope $P({\boldsymbol{M}})$ is called the flag matroid polytope of ${\boldsymbol{M}}$ ; we sometimes say it is a flag matroid polytope of rank $\mathbf{r}$ .

Flag matroids are exactly the type $A$ objects in the theory of Coxeter matroids [GS87, BGW03]. Just as a realization of a matroid is a point in a Grassmannian, a realization of a flag matroid is a point in a flag variety. More concretely, a realization of a flag matroid of ranks $(r_{1},\dots,r_{k})$ is an $r_{k}\times n$ matrix $A$ over a field such that for each $1\leq i\leq k$ , the $r_{i}\times n$ submatrix of $A$ formed by the first $r_{i}$ rows of $A$ is a realization of $M_{i}$ . For an equivalent definition of flag matroids in terms of Plücker relations on partial flag varieties, see [JL22, Proposition A].

There is a notion of moment map for any flag variety (indeed for any generalized partial flag variety $G/P$ ) [GS87, BGW03]. When a flag matroid ${\boldsymbol{M}}$ can be realized by a point $A$ in the flag variety, then its matroid polytope $P({\boldsymbol{M}})$ is the moment map image of the closure of the torus orbit of $A$ in the flag variety [GS87], [BGW03, Corollary 1.13.5].

There are natural “positive” analogues of matroids, flag matroids, and their polytopes.

#### Definition 1.2.

Let $\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\cdots,r_{k})$ be a sequence of increasing integers in $[n]$ . We say that a flag matroid $(M_{1},\dots,M_{k})$ of ranks $\mathbf{r}$ on $[n]$ is a flag positroid if it has a realization by a real matrix $A$ such that the $r_{i}\times n$ submatrix of $A$ formed by the first $r_{i}$ rows of $A$ has all nonnegative minors for each $1\leq i\leq k$ .

We refer to the flag matroid polytope of a flag positroid as a flag positroid polytope. It follows from our definition above that flag positroids are realizable.

Setting $k=1$ in Definition 1.2 gives the well-studied notion of positroids and positroid polytopes [Pos, Oh08, ARW16]. Therefore each flag positroid is a sequence of positroids.

In recent years it has been gradually understood that the tropical geometry of the Grassmannian and flag variety, and in particular, the Dressian and flag Dressian, are intimately connected to (flag) matroid polytopes and their subdivisions [Spe08, HJJS08, BEZ21] (see also [MS15, §4]). A particularly attractive point of view, which sheds light on the above connections, is the theory of (flag) matroids over hyperfields [BB19, JL22]. In this framework, the Dressian and flag Dressian are the Grassmannian and flag variety over the tropical hyperfield, while matroids and flag matroids are the points of the Grassmannian and flag variety over the Krasner hyperfield.

The tropical geometry of the positive Grassmannian and flag variety are particularly nice: the positive tropical Grassmannian equals the positive Dressian, whose cones in turn parameterize subdivisions of the hypersimplex into positroid polytopes [SW05, SW21, LPW20, AHLS20]. And the positive tropical complete flag variety equals the positive complete flag Dressian, whose cones parameterize subdivisions of the permutohedron into Bruhat interval polytopes [Bor22, JLLO]. Theorem A below unifies and generalizes the above results.

#### Definition 1.3.

Let $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the set underlying the tropical hyperfield, endowed with the topology such that $-\log:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{T}$ is a homeomorphism. Given a point $w\in\mathbb{T}^{\binom{[n]}{r}}$ , we define the support of $w$ to be $\underline{w}=\{S\in\binom{[n]}{r}:w_{S}\neq\infty\}$ . When $\underline{w}$ is the set of bases of a matroid, we identify $\underline{w}$ with that matroid. Let $\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{T}^{\binom{[n]}{r}}\right)$ be the tropical projective space of $\mathbb{T}^{\binom{[n]}{r}}$ , which is defined as $\big(\mathbb{T}^{\binom{[n]}{r}}\setminus\{(\infty,\ldots,\infty)\}\big)/\sim$ , where $w\sim w^{\prime}$ if $w=w^{\prime}+(c,\ldots,c)$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ .

Our main result is the following.

#### Theorem A.

Suppose $\mathbf{r}$ is a sequence of consecutive integers $(a,\ldots,b)$ for some $1\leq a\leq b\leq n$ . Then, for ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}=(\mu_{a},\ldots,\mu_{b})\in\prod_{i=a}^{b}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{T}^{\binom{[n]}{i}}\right)$ , the following statements are equivalent:

- (a) ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\TrFl_{\mathbf{r},n}^{\geq 0}$ , the nonnegative tropicalization of the flag variety, i.e. the closure of the coordinate-wise valuation of points in $\Fl_{\mathbf{r},n}(\mathcal{C}_{\geq 0})$ .

- (b) ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\FlDr_{\mathbf{r},n}^{\geq 0}$ , the nonnegative flag Dressian, i.e. the “solutions" to the positive-tropical Grassmann-Plücker and incidence-Plücker relations.

- (c) Every face in the coherent subdivision $\mathcal{D}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ of the polytope $P(\underline{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}})=P(\underline{\mu_{1}})+\cdots+P(\underline{\mu_{k}})$ induced by ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ is a flag positroid polytope (of rank $\mathbf{r}$ ).

- (d) Every face of dimension at most 2 in the subdivision $\mathcal{D}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ of $P(\underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}})$ is a flag positroid polytope (of rank $\mathbf{r}$ ).

- (e) The support $\underline{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$ of ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ is a flag matroid, ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ satisfies every three-term positive-tropical incidence relation when $a<b$ (respectively, every three-term positive-tropical Grassmann-Plücker relation when $a=b$ ), and either $\underline{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$ consists of uniform matroids or $\mu_{i}\in\Dr_{i;n}^{\geq 0}$ for at least one $a\leq i\leq b$ .

For the definitions of the objects in Theorem A, see Proposition 3.6 for (a), Definition 3.3 for (b), Definition 5.1 for (c), and Definition 3.8 for (e).

We note that if $\mathbf{r}=(d)$ is a single integer, Theorem A describes the relationship between the nonnegative tropical Grassmannian, the nonnegative Dressian, and subdivisions of positroid polytopes (e.g. the hypersimplex, if ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ has no coordinates equal to $\infty$ ) into positroid polytopes. And when $\mathbf{r}=(1,2,\dots,n)$ , Theorem A describes the relationship between the nonnegative tropical complete flag variety, the nonnegative complete flag Dressian, and subdivisions of Bruhat interval polytopes (e.g. the permutohedron, if ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ has no coordinates equal to $\infty$ ) into Bruhat interval polytopes. We illustrate this relationship in the case where ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ has no coordinates equal to $\infty$ in Figure 1.
