#### Proposition 4.27.

The following holds

$$ \mathbb{S}_{n}^{\geq 0}=\bigsqcup_{v\in W_{[n-1]}}\mathcal{R}_{v,w}^{>0} $$

#### Proof.

The set of positive skew-symmetric matrices $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{>0}$ is in bijection with the set of points in $\mathrm{OGr}^{\geq 0}(n,2n)$ represented by matrices $X$ that can be row reduced to the form $\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{Id}_{n}|A\end{bmatrix}$ . For this, we must have that the minor of the first $n$ columns of $X$ is nonzero. That is, there must be a path collection from $[n]$ to $[n]$ in the graph $G_{v,w}$ . By Corollary 4.22, this is possible if and only if the source vertices on the bottommost $n$ strands are $[n]$ . This happens when $v^{-1}([n])=[n]$ , equivalently $v([n])=[n]$ , which is exactly the condition that $v\in W_{[n-1]}$ . ∎

## 5 Pfaffian signs

We recall that the determinant $\det(A)$ of a skew-symmetric matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2m}$ of size $2m\times 2m$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2m$ in the entries of $A$ . Moreover, it is the square of a degree $m$ homogeneous polynomial $\mathrm{Pf}(A)$ known as the Pfaffian,

$$ \mathrm{Pf}(A):=\frac{1}{2^{m}m!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2m}}{\rm sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{m}a_{\sigma(2i-1),\sigma(2i)}. $$

For any skew-symmetric matrix $A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}$ and any set $I\subset[n]$ of even size we denote by $\mathrm{Pf}_{I}(A)$ the pfaffian of the submarix $A_{I}$ of $A$ whose rows and column indices are in $I$ . By convention, we set $\mathrm{Pf}_{\emptyset}(A)=1$ . We denote the semi-algebraic set of Pfaffian-positive skew-symmetric matrices by

$$ \mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}>0}\coloneqq\Big\{A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}:\sgn(I,[n])\ \mathrm{Pf}_{I}(A)>0\quad\text{for any }I\subset[n]\text{ of even size}\Big\}, $$

and denote by $\mathbb{S}^{\mathrm{Pf}\geq 0}_{n}$ its Euclidean closure in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ .

#### Remark 5.1.

Let $g={\rm diag}(1,-1,1\dots,(-1)^{n+1})$ . We note that a skew-symmetric matrix $A$ is in $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}>0}$ if and only if $\mathrm{Pf}_{I}(A^{\prime})>0$ for any subset $I\subset[n]$ of even size where $A^{\prime}=gAg^{T}$ . So the set $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}>0}$ is conjugate to set of matrices with positive pfaffians. This justifies our notation.

A priori, there is no reason why the notion of total positivity in $\mathbb{S}_{n}$ we have discussed so far should be compatible with $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}>0}$ . In this section, we briefly discuss how these two notions of positivity are related, namely we prove Theorem 1.7 and discuss a few consequences. To do so, we shall need some background on the half-spin representation. For more details on Lie theoretic background we refer the reader to [23, 37].

Recall the vector spaces $E$ and $F$ from (2) and let $V=E\oplus F\cong\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ . The space $V$ is equipped with the quadratic form $q$ as in (1). The exterior algebra $\bigwedge^{\bullet}E$ decomposes into a direct sum of two vector spaces $\bigwedge^{\bullet}E=S\oplus S^{-}$ , where $S$ (resp. $S^{-}$ ) is the subspace of elements in $\bigwedge^{\bullet}E$ of degree equal to $n$ (resp. $n+1$ ) modulo 2. For any $I=\{i_{1}<\ldots<i_{\ell}\}\subset[n]$ we denote $e_{I}:=e_{i_{1}}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_{\ell}}$ . The $2^{n-1}$ vectors $e_{[n]\setminus I}$ where $I$ is a subset of $[n]$ of even size form a basis of $S$ .

The orthogonal Grassmannian $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ can be minimally embedded as the Spinor variety in $\mathbb{P}(S)$ . Here, we briefly explain how this embedding is obtained using Pfaffians. Following [34, Section 2] and [37, Section 11.7], let $\mathscr{C}$ be the Clifford algebra of the quadratic space $(V,q)$ . This algebra is defined as the quotient of the tensor algebra $T^{\bullet}V$ modulo the relations

$$ u\otimes v+v\otimes u=2q(u,v),\quad\text{for }u,v\in V. $$

Let $f:=f_{1}\cdots f_{n}\in\mathscr{C}$ and note that the left-ideal $\mathscr{C}\cdot f$ is isomorphic (as a vector space) to $\wedge^{\bullet}E$ via $e_{I}\cdot f\mapsto e_{I}$ . Now, let $A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}$ and $H=\mathrm{rowspan}\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{Id}_{n}|A\end{bmatrix}$ . Then, $H$ is spanned by

$$ e_{i}(A):=e_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}f_{j},\quad\text{for }1\leq i\leq n. $$

Let $h=e_{1}(A)\cdots e_{n}(A)\in\mathscr{C}$ , then the pure spinor of $A$ , namely the point in $\mathbb{P}(S)$ that represents $H$ , is the one dimensional linear space $h\mathscr{C}\cap\mathscr{C}f$ in $\mathscr{C}f\cong\wedge^{\bullet}E$ , see [13, III.1.1]. The line $h\mathscr{C}\cap\mathscr{C}f$ in $S$ is spanned over $\mathbb{C}$ by $h\cdot f\in\mathscr{C}\cdot f$ . In other words, the pure spinor of $A$ is the element $u_{H}\in\bigwedge^{\bullet}E$ such that of $u_{H}\cdot f=h\cdot f$ .

#### Lemma 5.2.

Given a generic point in $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ of the form $\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{Id}_{n}|A\end{bmatrix}$ with $A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}$ , the corresponding pure Spinor in $\mathbb{P}(S)$ is

$$ \sum_{I\subset[n]\text{ of even size}}\sgn(I,[n])\ 2^{|I|/2}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{I}(A)\ e_{[n]\setminus I}\quad\in S. $$

#### Proof.

It is enough to compute $h\cdot f$ in $\mathscr{C}$ . We proceed by induction on $n$ . Suppose the result holds for all $A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}$ . Fix $A=(a_{i,j})_{i,j=1}^{n+1}\in\mathbb{S}_{n+1}$ and let us write

$$ u_{i}:=e_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}f_{j}\quad\text{for }1\leq i\leq n+1. $$

Note that for any $1\leq i\leq n+1$ and $1\leq j\leq n$ we have $f_{i}^{2}=0$ and $f_{n+1}u_{j}=-u_{j}f_{n+1}$ . We then have

$$ \displaystyle e_{1}(A)\cdots e_{n}(A)\ e_{n+1}(A)\ f \displaystyle=e_{1}(A)\cdots e_{n}(A)\ e_{n+1}\ f \displaystyle=\left(u_{1}+a_{1,n+1}f_{n+1}\right)\cdots\left(u_{n}+a_{n,n+1}f_{n+1}\right)\ e_{n+1}\ f \displaystyle=\left(u_{1}\cdots u_{n}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}a_{i,n+1}u_{1}\cdots\widehat{u_{i}}\cdots u_{n}\ f_{n+1}\right)\ e_{n+1}\ f \displaystyle=u_{1}\cdots u_{n}\ e_{n+1}\ f+\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}a_{i,n+1}u_{1}\cdots\widehat{u_{i}}\cdots u_{n}\ f_{n+1}\ e_{n+1}\ f. $$

By the induction hypothesis, we have

$$ u_{1}\cdots u_{n}e_{n+1}f=\sum\limits_{K\subset[n]\text{ even}}{\rm sgn}(K,[n])\ 2^{|K|/2}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{K}(A)e_{[n+1]\setminus K}\ f. $$

Note that $f_{n+1}e_{n+1}\ f=(-e_{n+1}f_{n+1}\ +\ 2)\ f=2f$ . For each $i\in[n]$ we denote $A^{\prime}_{i}$ for the submatrix of $A$ with rows and columns $i,n+1$ removed. Then,

$$ u_{1}\cdots\widehat{u_{i}}\cdots u_{n}f=\sum_{K\subset[n]\setminus i\text{ even}}{\rm sgn}(K,[n+1])\ 2^{|K|/2}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{K}(A^{\prime}_{i})e_{[n]\setminus(K\cup i)}f. $$

Using the recursive formula for Pfaffians, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}a_{i,n+1}\ u_{1}\cdots\widehat{u_{i}}\cdots u_{n}\ f_{n+1}\ e_{n+1}\ f \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}\ 2\ a_{i,n+1}\ u_{1}\cdots\widehat{u_{i}}\cdots u_{n}f \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{K\subset[n]\setminus i\text{ even}}(-1)^{n-i}\ 2^{1+|K|/2}\ a_{i,n+1}{\rm sgn}(K,[n]\setminus i)\ \mathrm{Pf}_{K}(A^{\prime}_{i})\ e_{[n]\setminus(K\cup i)}\ f \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}K=\{i_{1}<\ldots<i_{l}\}\text{ even}\\
i_{l}=n+1\end{subarray}}{\rm sgn}(K,[n+1])2^{|K|/2}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{l-1}(-1)^{j}a_{i_{j},n+1}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{K\setminus\{i_{j},n+1\}}(A)\right)\ e_{[n+1]\setminus K}\ f \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}K\subset[n+1]\text{ even}\\
n+1\in K\end{subarray}}{\rm sgn}(K,[n+1])\ 2^{|K|/2}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{K}(A)\ e_{[n+1]\setminus K}\ f.\qed $$

We note that Equation 21 appears in [34, Section 2.3] up to a sign and constant inconsistency, which is not relevant for their purposes.

The vector space $S$ can be endowed with an action of the spin group $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$ . This is the half-spin representation. It is an irreducible representation corresponding to the highest weight vector $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}(1,\dots,1)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . The basis $\{e_{[n]\setminus I}:I\subset[n]\text{ of even size}\}$ is a basis of weight vectors of $S$ for this representation, and the weights of $S$ are $\frac{1}{2}\left(\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1\right)$ where the number of minus signs is even. Explicitly, the weight of $e_{[n]\setminus I}$ has $-$ in the positions indexed by $I$ , and in particular the highest weight vector is $e_{[n]}$ with weight $\lambda$ .

We now describe $S$ as a representation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{spin}(2n)\cong\mathfrak{so}(2n)=\bigwedge^{2}V$ . Following [13, Chapter II] and [30, Section 5] the action of $\mathfrak{so}(2n)$ on $S$ is given as follows. For $v=v^{\prime}\oplus v^{\prime\prime}\in E\oplus F$ and $\omega=\omega_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\omega_{k}\in\bigwedge^{k}E$ , we write

$$ v\cdot\omega:=v^{\prime}\wedge\omega_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\omega_{k}+2\sum_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{i-1}q(v^{\prime\prime},\omega_{i})\ \omega_{1}\wedge\cdots\omega_{i-1}\wedge\omega_{i+1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\omega_{k}. $$

Note that $v\cdot\omega\in\bigwedge^{k-1}E\oplus\bigwedge^{k+1}E$ . Then for $\omega\in S$ we have $v\cdot\omega\in S^{-}$ . Acting again with another element $w\in V$ yields $w\cdot(v\cdot\omega)\in S$ . Hence we obtain an action of $\mathfrak{so}(2n)$ on $S$ :

$$ (v_{1}\wedge v_{2})\cdot\omega=\frac{1}{4}[v_{1},v_{2}]\cdot\omega=\frac{1}{4}(v_{1}\cdot(v_{2}\cdot\omega)-v_{2}\cdot(v_{1}\cdot\omega))\quad\text{for any }v\wedge w\in\mathfrak{so}(2n)\text{ and }\omega\in S. $$

The factor of $1/4$ comes from the degree $2$ covering map $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)\to\mathrm{SO}(2n)$ .

The $2^{n-1}$ Pfaffians of $A$ are related to certain regular functions on $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ known as generalized minors. These functions are positive on $\mathrm{OGr}^{>0}(n,2n)$ , see [35, Lemma 11.4]. To define them we need to fix the root space decomposition of $\mathfrak{so}(2n)$ . The maximal torus (6) of $\mathrm{SO}(2n)$ corresponds to a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}$ of $\mathfrak{so}(2n)$ . We identify the dual $\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}$ of $\mathfrak{h}$ with the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{n}=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{n})$ . The action of the Weyl group $W$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is given through its generators (8) as follows

$$ s_{i}\cdot(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})=\begin{cases}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{i-1},a_{i+1},a_{i},a_{i+2},\ldots,a_{n})&\text{if }1\leq i\leq n-1,\\
(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-2},-a_{n},-a_{n-1})&\text{if }i=n.\end{cases} $$

We choose a set of simple roots $\Phi=\{\varepsilon_{1}-\varepsilon_{2},\varepsilon_{2}-\varepsilon_{3},\ldots,\varepsilon_{n-1}-\varepsilon_{n},\varepsilon_{n-1}+\varepsilon_{n}\}$ . The positive roots are then

$$ \Phi^{+}=\{\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j}:1\leq i<j\leq n\}\cup\{\varepsilon_{i}+\varepsilon_{j}:1\leq i,j\leq n\}. $$

Finally, we note that the following roots and their root vectors correspond to the pinning in Section 2 by taking the matrix exponential $\exp:\mathfrak{so}(2n)\cong\wedge^{2}\mathbb{C}^{2n}\to\mathrm{SO}(2n)$ :

| Roots | $\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j}$ for $i\neq j$ | $\varepsilon_{i}+\varepsilon_{j}$ for $i\leq j$ | $-\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j}$ for $i\leq j$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Root vectors | $e_{i}\wedge f_{j}$ | $e_{i}\wedge e_{j}$ | $f_{j}\wedge f_{i}$ |

*Table 1. The roots of $\mathfrak{so}(2n)$ and their corresponding root vectors in the half spin representation $S$ .*

Recall the definition of $\dot{s}_{i}$ from (16).

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $I$ be a subset of $[n]$ of even size. Then for $1\leq i\leq n-1$ ,

$$ {\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{i})\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}=\begin{cases}-\frac{\pi}{2}e_{[n]\setminus((I\setminus i)\cup i+1)}\quad&\text{if }i\in I\text{ and }i+1\not\in I,\\
\frac{\pi}{2}e_{[n]\setminus((I\setminus i+1)\cup i)}\quad&\text{if }i\not\in I\text{ and }i+1\in I,\\
0\quad&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} $$

and

$$ {\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{n})\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}=\begin{cases}\frac{-\pi}{4}e_{[n]\setminus(I\setminus\{n-1,n\})}\quad&\text{if }n\in I\text{ and }n+1\in I,\\
\pi e_{[n]\setminus(I\cup\{n-1,n\})}\quad&\text{if }n\not\in I\text{ and }n+1\not\in I,\\
0\quad&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Here, ${\rm Log}\colon{\rm Spin}(2n)\to\mathfrak{spin}(2n)$ is the logarithm map between a simply connected Lie group and its Lie algebra.

#### Proof.

Using a matrix logarithm for the root subgroup corresponding to $s_{i}$ in ${\rm Spin}(2n)$ yields the following formula for ${\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{i})\in\mathfrak{spin}(2n)\cong\wedge^{2}(E\oplus F)$ :

$$ {\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{i})=\begin{cases}\frac{\pi}{2}(e_{i+1}\wedge f_{i}-e_{i}\wedge f_{i+1})&\text{if }1\leq i\leq n-1,\\
\frac{\pi}{2}(f_{n}\wedge f_{n-1}-e_{n-1}\wedge e_{n})&\text{if }i=n.\end{cases} $$

Note that, for $I\subset[n]$ of even size, we have for any $i,j\in[n]$

$$ \displaystyle e_{i}\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{\sgn(i,I\setminus i)}e_{[n]\setminus(I\setminus i)},&\text{ if }i\in I,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} \displaystyle f_{j}\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}=2\begin{cases}(-1)^{\sgn(j,I)}e_{[n]\setminus(I\cup j)},&\text{ if }j\notin I,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

The following computation gives the desired result for ${\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{i})\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}$ . A similar computation yields the result for $\dot{s}_{n}$ .

$$ \displaystyle(e_{i+1}\wedge f_{i}-e_{i}\wedge f_{i+1})\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}=\frac{1}{4}\left(e_{i+1}f_{i}-f_{i}e_{i+1}-e_{i}f_{i+1}+f_{i+1}e_{i}\right)\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(e_{i+1}f_{i}-e_{i}f_{i+1}\right)\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I}=\begin{cases}-e_{[n]\setminus((I\setminus i)\cup i+1)}&\text{if }i\in I\text{ and }i+1\not\in I,\\
e_{[n]\setminus((I\setminus i+1)\cup i)}\quad&\text{if }i\not\in I\text{ and }i+1\in I,\\
0\quad&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.7.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.7.

Given a skew-symmetric matrix $A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}$ , the Pfaffians of $A$ are, up to fixed scalars, an instance of generalized minors of the point $[\mathrm{Id}_{n}|A]$ in $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ for the half-spin representation $S$ . Following [13, Section III, 1.3-1.7], we know that if $g\in\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$ is a lift of an element $\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{Id}_{n}&\ast\\ A&\ast\end{bmatrix}$ of $\mathrm{SO}(2n)$ where $A\in\mathbb{S}_{n}$ , then $g\cdot e_{[n]}$ is the pure spinor corresponding to the rowspan of $\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{Id}_{n}|A\end{bmatrix}$ . Thus, by Lemma 5.2,

$$ g\cdot e_{[n]}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subset[n]\\
|I|\text{ even}\end{subarray}}\sgn(I,[n])\ 2^{|I|/2}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{I}(A)\ e_{[n]\setminus I}. $$

Note that the change from row to columns convention is due to Remark 2.1. The generalized minors corresponding to the half-spin representation $S$ are given by

$$ m_{w}(g)=\langle g\cdot e_{[n]},\dot{w}\cdot e_{[n]}\rangle, $$

where $\dot{w}\in\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$ is a lift of $w\in W$ to the Spin group, and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the standard inner product with respect to the basis $(e_{[n]\setminus I})$ of $S$ . We stress that this lifting depends on the choice of a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}$ , the simple roots, and root vectors made previously for $\mathfrak{so}(2n)$ , that is, a pinning of $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$ compatible with that of $\mathrm{SO}(2n)$ in Section 2.

Recall from Definition 4.15 that $I_{w}:=\{i\in[n]:w(i)>n\}$ .

#### Lemma 5.4.

For any $w\in W$ we have

$$ \dot{w}\cdot e_{[n]}=c_{w}\ e_{[n]\setminus I_{w^{-1}}},\quad\text{for some nonzero scalar }c_{w}\in\mathbb{R}. $$

#### Proof.

A classical result from the representation theory of Lie algebras [25, Section 7.2 and Lemma 21.3] guarantees that for any $w\in W$ , the vector $\dot{w}\cdot e_{[n]}$ is a weight vector of weight $w\cdot\lambda$ , where $\lambda$ is the highest weight. Hence, it is enough to show that $w\cdot\lambda$ has $-\frac{1}{2}$ in the positions indexed by the set $I_{w^{-1}}$ . By equation (22), $w\in W$ acts on $\lambda$ by applying a signed permutation. Observe that when we apply $w$ to $\lambda=(\frac{1}{2},\cdots,\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\cdots,-\frac{1}{2})$ , we have $w^{-1}(i)>n$ if and only if $(w\cdot\lambda)_{i}<0$ . Since all the weight spaces of $S$ are one-dimensional, we obtain $\dot{w}\cdot e_{[n]}=c_{w}\ e_{[n]\setminus I_{w^{-1}}}$ , where $c_{w}\in\mathbb{R}$ as desired. ∎

Hence, from (23), we deduce that

$$ m_{w}(g)=\langle g\cdot e_{[n]},\dot{w}\cdot e_{[n]}\rangle=c_{w}\sgn(I_{w^{-1}},[n])\ 2^{|I_{w^{-1}}|/2}\ \mathrm{Pf}_{I_{w^{-1}}}(A). $$

Then, by [35, Lemma 11.4] (and, indirectly, by [33, Theorem 3.4]), it is enough to prove that the scalars $c_{w}$ are positive. To do so we first need the following.

From Remark 4.16 there is a bijection $wW_{[n-1]}\mapsto W_{[n-1]}w^{-1}\mapsto I_{w^{-1}}$ between left cosets of $W_{[n-1]}$ and even subsets of $[n]$ . Hence, it is enough to consider the minimal representatives of left-cosets in $W/W_{[n-1]}$ to obtain all Pfaffians as generalized minors.

We now prove inductively on the length of $w\in W^{[n-1]}$ that $c_{w}>0$ . For $\ell(w)=0$ , $w={\rm id}$ and $I_{w^{-1}}=\emptyset$ . Then, we have the desired sign because $c_{\rm id}=1$ . Assume that $c_{w^{\prime}}>0$ and let $w=s_{i}\ w^{\prime}$ , for some $i\in[n]$ . Since $w^{\prime}$ is a minimal left coset representative, $w$ is as well. We have $\dot{w}\cdot e_{[n]}=\dot{s}_{i}\ \dot{w}^{\prime}\cdot e_{[n]}=c_{w^{\prime}}\ \dot{s}_{i}\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}}$ . As we are considering a representation of the simply connected group of type $D_{n}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$ , we have $\dot{s}_{i}\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}}=\exp({\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{i}))\cdot e_{[n]\setminus I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}}$ .

Since $\ell(w^{\prime})=\ell(w)-1$ , $(w^{\prime})^{-1}(\alpha_{i})$ is a positive root. If $1\leq i\leq n-1$ , this means $(w^{\prime})^{-1}\varepsilon_{i}-(w^{\prime})^{-1}\varepsilon_{i+1}>0$ . However, since $w$ and $w^{\prime}$ are minimal coset representatives, $I_{w^{-1}}\neq I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}$ and so either $i\in I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}$ or $i+1\in I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}$ , but not both. Thus, $i+1\in I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}$ and $i\notin I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}$ , that is, $I_{w^{-1}}=(I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}\setminus\{i+1\})\cup\{i\}$ . If $i=n$ , since $|I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}|$ is even, $(w^{\prime})^{-1}\alpha_{n}>0$ implies $n-1,n\notin I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}$ . In this case, $I_{w^{-1}}=I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}\cup\{n-1,n\}$ .

By Lemma 5.3, $\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(e_{[n]\setminus I_{(w^{\prime})^{-1}}},e_{[n]\setminus I_{w^{-1}})}$ is invariant under the action of ${\rm Log}(\dot{s}_{i})$ . We can calculate the corresponding action of $\dot{s}_{i}$ via the matrix exponential, obtaining $c_{w}=c_{w^{\prime}}$ if $i\in[n-1]$ and $c_{w}=2c_{w^{\prime}}$ if $i=n$ . ∎

#### Example 5.5.

The matrix $A$ in Example 4.2 is manifestly not nonnegative as its Pfaffians do not satisfy the sign pattern in Theorem 1.7. Indeed the entry $(3,4)$ of $A$ is $-2<0$ .

#### Example 5.6.

We have shown that $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}\geq 0}$ . This inclusion is strict. For example

$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0&2\\
0&0&1&0\\
0&-1&0&2\\
-2&0&-2&0\end{bmatrix} $$

belongs in $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}\geq 0}$ . However, using Theorem 1.5 as in Example 4.2, one can check that the minors $M_{j,k}(B(\epsilon))$ are

$$ \displaystyle 8\,\epsilon+o(\epsilon^{2}),\quad \displaystyle 16\,\epsilon+o(\epsilon^{2}), \displaystyle 8\,\epsilon+o(\epsilon^{2}), \displaystyle 2+o(\epsilon^{2}),\quad \displaystyle\mathbf{-2}+o(\epsilon^{2}), \displaystyle 2+o(\epsilon). $$

Thus, the matrix $A$ is not nonnegative.

## 6 Future directions

### 6.1 Cluster structure

The connection between positivity and cluster algebras has arisen frequently since the seminal works of Bernstein, Fomin and Zelevinsky, see for example [7]. Consequently, whenever there is a positivity test for a semi-algebraic region of a projective variety in terms of regular functions, it is natural to ask whether they form a cluster in some cluster algebra. The cluster algebra structure of partial flag varieties was described in general in [20] using the language of cluster categories, but it is difficult to infer whether it relates to the minors $M_{j,k}$ in the case of the orthogonal Grassmannian. We briefly comment on how the relationship between positivity and cluster structures on the orthogonal Grassmannian $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ compares to related varieties.

Recent work of Bossinger and Li [11] explored cluster structures on partial flag varieties of type A, giving an explicit interpretation of the cluster structure in [20]. Bossinger and Li describe how to obtain the cluster structure on two specific families of partial flag varieties from the cluster structure on a Grassmannian and conjecture this can be done more generally. In particular, starting from an initial quiver for the Grassmannian, they give a sequence of mutations, freezings of mutable vertices, and deletions of vertices that transform it into a quiver of the partial flag variety cluster algebra. Since positivity of the variables in a single cluster guarantees positivity of all cluster variables, this work provides a cluster theoretic grounding for the positivity test described in [9] and can be interpreted as conjecturally giving an explicit positivity test for any (type A) partial flag variety. In this setting, all Plücker coordinates are cluster variables and thus are positive on the positive flag variety.

We now turn to $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ . Unlike the type A setting, our positivity asks that a set of Plücker coordinates have a fixed sign pattern, so that some coordinates are forced to be negative. Moreover, there exist Plücker coordinates whose sign is not fixed on the positive orthogonal Grassmannian. In Example 2.3 we described the open Deodehar component in $\mathrm{OGr}(4,8)$ ; the Plücker coordinate $\Delta^{1458}(X)=t_{1}^{2}t_{2}^{2}t_{3}t_{4}-t_{1}t_{2}t_{3}t_{4}t_{5}t_{6}$ has indeterminate sign for $t_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ . We remark there are similar behaviors in the BCFW tiles of the $(n,k,m=4)$ amplituhedron [16]. Using signed seeds, the authors of [16] are still able to obtain the cluster structure on a standard BCFW tile from a seed of the cluster structure on $\mathrm{Gr}(4,n)$ by freezing certain variables, where the Plücker coordinates whose signs are not fixed on the tiles do not appear as cluster variables. This could offer a hint of how to proceed in the case of the orthogonal Grassmannian.

### 6.2 Positroids

One could try to study orthogonal positroids of rank $n$ . Positroids are rich combinatorial objects, which can be concisely described in terms of many familiar structures, including (decorated) permutations, (matroid) polytopes, planar (bi-colored) graphs, and (Le-diagrams on) tableaux. Let $\mathbb{k}$ be a field and let $X\in\mathbb{k}^{\binom{n}{k}}$ have coordinates $\Delta^{I}(X)$ indexed by $\binom{[n]}{k}$ . Define the support of $X$ as ${\rm supp}(X)=\{I\colon\Delta^{I}(X)\neq 0\}$ . Then, the rank $k$ positroids on $[n]$ are $\{{\rm supp}(X)\colon X\in\mathrm{Gr}^{\geq 0}(k,n)\}$ . These are in bijection with cells in the Richardson decomposition of $\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)$ . Points of the Grassmannian over the sign hyperfield $\mathscr{S}$ , in the sense of [5], are called oriented matroids. By [1, 38], positively oriented matroids, that is, those with all coordinates equal to $1$ or $0$ , are in bijection with positroids; If we extend the definition of support to allow $\mathbb{k}$ to be a hyperfield, then positroids are precisely the supports of positively oriented matroids. To generalize this story, we can analogously define orthogonal positroids of rank $n$ to be $\{{\rm supp}(X)\colon X\in\mathrm{OGr}^{\geq 0}(n,2n)\}$ . We note that $\mathrm{OGr}(n,2n)$ is cut out by Plücker relations and by some additional relations $\mathcal{S}$ equating certain Plücker coordinates (possibly with a sign). We propose the following definitions.

#### Definition 6.1.

The orthogonal Grassmannian $\mathrm{OGr}_{\mathscr{H}}(n,2n)$ over a hyperfield $\mathscr{H}$ is the subset of the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(n,2n)$ over $\mathscr{H}$ consisting of points which satisfy $\mathcal{S}$ .

#### Definition 6.2.

We say a point of $\mathrm{OGr}_{\mathscr{H}}(n,2n)$ is a (rank $n$ ) orthogonal oriented matroid on $2n$ elements.

As in our consideration of cluster algebra structures, we need to be careful since not all Plücker coordinates have a fixed sign on the nonnegative orthogonal Grassmannian. For each $\epsilon=(\epsilon_{I})\in\{-1,1\}^{\binom{2n}{n}}$ indexed by $\binom{[2n]}{n}$ , let

$$ \mathrm{OGr}_{\mathscr{S}}^{\epsilon}(n,2n)=\left\{\Delta^{I}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{\binom{2n}{n}}\in\mathrm{OGr}_{\mathscr{S}}(n,2n)\colon\epsilon_{I}\Delta^{I}\in\{0,1\}\text{ for each }I\in\binom{[2n]}{n}\right\}. $$

#### Definition 6.3.

We say that an oriented orthogonal matroid in $\mathrm{OGr}_{\mathscr{S}}^{\epsilon}(n,2n)$ is an orthogonal $\epsilon$ -oriented matroid.

It is straightforward to show that there exists $\epsilon$ such that each orthogonal positroid is the support of an orthogonal $\epsilon$ -oriented matroid. However, it is not clear if there are choices of $\epsilon$ for which the converse holds.

Finally, while there are type D Le diagrams as constructed in [29], there are many questions to explore surrounding the combinatorics of orthogonal positroids. Concretely, one may ask if there exist objects generalizing decorated permutations, matroid polytopes, plabic graphs, or other familiar positroid cryptomorphisms which admit nice combinatorial descriptions and are in bijection with the Richardson cells $\mathcal{R}_{v,w^{[n-1]}}$ .

### 6.3 Related semi-algebraic sets

In the beginning of this article, we made a choice of the quadratic form $q$ . However, besides connecting the orthogonal Grassmannian to skew-symmetric matrices, this choice was somewhat arbitrary and our result translates nicely to other quadratic forms of signature $(n,n)$ . Explicitly, changing quadratic forms is the same as doing a change of basis, and if we also shift the pinning by the same change of bases, we obtain a shifted positivity test. We denote by $\mathrm{OGr}_{q}(n,2n)$ (resp. $\mathrm{OGr}^{\geq 0}_{q}(n,2n)$ ) the orthogonal Grassmannian (resp. nonnegative orthogonal Grassmannian) for the quadratic form $q$ . Another natural choice of quadratic form we may consider is

$$ q^{\prime}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\xrightarrow{}\mathbb{R},\quad x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{2n}(-1)^{i+1}x_{i}^{2}. $$

The standard component of $\mathrm{OGr}_{q^{\prime}}(n,2n)$ is cut out by the Plücker relations and the additional linear relations

$$ \Delta^{I}(X)=\Delta^{[2n]\setminus I}(X),\quad\text{for all }I\in\binom{[2n]}{n}. $$

The Plücker non-negative semi-algebraic set in $\mathrm{OGr}_{q^{\prime}}(n,2n)$ emerged as the geometry behind the ABJM amplitudes in [24, 27] and, in [18], it was connected to the Ising model in statistical mechanics. This semi-algebraic set is rather different from $\mathrm{OGr}^{\geq 0}_{q^{\prime}}(n,2n)$ . It particular, it turns out that some Plücker coordinates do not even have a fixed sign in $\mathrm{OGr}^{\geq 0}_{q^{\prime}}(n,2n)$ .

More generally, the notion of total positivity introduced by Lusztig for flag varieties only coincides with the positivity of Plücker coordinates in special cases, see [6]. In many cases, the geometry that is relevant to applications, for example in physics, is the semi-algebraic set where certain regular functions are positive. In the cases where the notion of positivity we are interested in does not coincide with the notion of total positivity it generally becomes hard to find combinatorial structures which explain the boundary stratification of the semi-algebraic set of interest. An example of such a situation is $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\mathrm{Pf}\geq 0}$ which is interesting to study in its own right. As the structure stops being governed by the combinatorics of the Weyl group, other tools are necessary to study its cell decomposition. Also, as briefly explained in Section 5, this is closely related to considering a positive Spinor variety. We leave these questions for future work.
